note: Nutrition research, eight narrow briefs run on the PubMed connector. Every claim carries a PMID that was retrieved and then independently re-checked with get_article_metadata in batches of six: 150 of 150 exist. Every claim carries a verbatim quote from the abstract actually retrieved. The recurring gap, recorded per topic rather than assumed: essentially none of this literature includes people using anabolic compounds or on hormone therapy — zero trials pair a GLP-1 with testosterone, zero pair creatine with AAS. The numbers are real; the population is not this app's. NOT verified: no independent second reader has re-checked the quotes against their abstracts.

claims.statement: In people already on blood-pressure medication, cutting dietary sodium still lowers blood pressure substantially, and the size of the drop is proportional to how much sodium comes out of the diet.
claims.amount: Every 100 mmol/day reduction in 24-h urinary sodium (~2.3 g sodium, ~5.8 g salt) lowered systolic BP by 6.81 mmHg (95% CI 4.96-8.66) and diastolic BP by 3.85 mmHg (95% CI 2.26-5.43); median trial duration 28 days.
claims.population: 2,885 adults with hypertension already on stable blood-pressure-lowering medication, pooled from 35 randomised controlled trials of >=2 weeks with 24-h urinary sodium verification.
claims.quote: For every 100 mmol reduction in 24-hour urinary sodium excretion, systolic blood pressure decreased by 6.81 mm Hg (95% CI, 4.96-8.66), diastolic blood pressure decreased by 3.85 mm Hg (95% CI, 2.26-5.43), and mean arterial pressure decreased by 4.83 mm Hg (95% CI, 3.22-6.44).

claims.statement: A realistic, sustainable salt cut of roughly one teaspoon a day lowers blood pressure in four weeks or more, with about twice the effect in people whose blood pressure is already high as in people whose blood pressure is normal.
claims.amount: A 75 mmol/24 h reduction in urinary sodium (equivalent to 4.4 g/day less salt) lowered systolic BP by 4.18 mmHg (95% CI -5.18 to -3.18) and diastolic BP by 2.06 mmHg (-2.67 to -1.45). In hypertensive people the systolic fall was 5.39 mmHg; in normotensive people 2.42 mmHg.
claims.population: 3,230 adults (hypertensive and normotensive, both sexes, white and black participants) in 34 randomised trials of modest salt reduction lasting at least four weeks.
claims.quote: Meta-analysis showed that the mean change in urinary sodium (reduced salt v usual salt) was -75 mmol/24 h (equivalent to a reduction of 4.4 g/day salt), and with this reduction in salt intake, the mean change in blood pressure was -4.18 mm Hg (95% confidence interval -5.18 to -3.18, I(2)=75%) for systolic blood pressure and -2.06 mm Hg (-2.67 to -1.45, I(2)=68%) for diastolic blood pressure.

claims.statement: Cutting salt is a blood-pressure lever only: it does not move cholesterol or triglycerides at all, so anyone tracking a lipid panel should not expect sodium restriction to change it.
claims.amount: With a 4.4 g/day salt reduction, total cholesterol changed by +0.05 mmol/L (95% CI -0.02 to 0.11), LDL by +0.05 mmol/L (-0.01 to 0.12), HDL by -0.02 mmol/L (-0.06 to 0.01) and triglycerides by +0.04 mmol/L (-0.02 to 0.09) - all non-significant.
claims.population: Subset of the same 34 randomised salt-reduction trials (3,230 adults, hypertensive and normotensive) that also reported lipid and hormone outcomes.
claims.quote: Meta-analysis of data on hormones and lipids showed that the mean change was 0.26 ng/mL/h (0.17 to 0.36, I(2)=70%) for plasma renin activity, 73.20 pmol/L (44.92 to 101.48, I(2)=62%) for aldosterone, 187 pmol/L (39 to 336, I(2)=5%) for noradrenaline (norepinephrine), 37 pmol/L (-1 to 74, I(2)=12%) for adrenaline (epinephrine), 0.05 mmol/L (-0.02 to 0.11, I(2)=0%) for total cholesterol, 0.05 mmol/L (-0.01 to 0.12, I(2)=0%) for low density lipoprotein cholesterol, -0.02 mmol/L (-0.06 to 0.01, I(2)=16%) for high density lipoprotein cholesterol, and 0.04 mmol/L (-0.02 to 0.09, I(2)=0%) for triglycerides.

claims.statement: Potassium (the mineral behind salt substitutes and the DASH pattern's fruit and vegetables) helps blood pressure only up to a point - past a moderate dose the benefit disappears and, in people on blood-pressure drugs, blood pressure went back up.
claims.amount: Benefit weakened above an active-vs-control difference of 30 mmol/day in potassium excretion, and blood pressure rose above a difference of roughly 80 mmol/day; trial doses ranged 30-140 mmol/day. The rise was seen only in drug-treated hypertensive participants.
claims.population: Participants in 32 randomised controlled trials of potassium supplementation lasting >=4 weeks, mostly adults with hypertension, some on antihypertensive drugs and some untreated.
claims.quote: We observed a U-shaped relationship between 24-hour active and control arm differences in potassium excretion and BP levels, with weakening of the BP reduction effect above differences of 30 mmol/d and a BP increase above differences ≈80 mmol/d. Achieved potassium excretion analysis also identified a U-shaped relationship. The BP-lowering effects of potassium supplementation were stronger in participants with hypertension and at higher levels of sodium intake. The BP increase with high potassium excretion was noted in participants with antihypertensive drug-treated hypertension but not in their untreated counterparts.
claims.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

claims.statement: Combining the DASH eating pattern with sodium restriction lowers blood pressure, but only when the food is actually supplied - trials that just taught people the pattern produced no measurable blood-pressure change.
claims.amount: Across eight trials, systolic effect sizes ranged from -7.7 to -2.4 mmHg and diastolic from -8.3 to +0.1 mmHg. BP fell significantly in 2 of 3 feeding studies, 1 of 3 food-provision studies, and 0 of 3 education-only studies.
claims.population: Adults aged 18 and over in nine randomised controlled trials of a sodium-restricted DASH diet, delivered as feeding, food provision, or education.
claims.quote: BP was significantly reduced in two of the three feeding studies, one of the three provisional studies and none of the educational studies. In eight studies, effect sizes varied among both systolic BP (-7·7 to -2·4) and diastolic BP (-8·3 to 0·1). Six studies showed an overall high risk of bias.

claims.statement: The DASH pattern is one of the few single dietary changes that moves blood pressure and cholesterol at the same time, and it works harder in people who start with worse numbers.
claims.amount: Systolic BP -5.2 mmHg (95% CI -7.0 to -3.4), diastolic BP -2.6 mmHg (-3.5 to -1.7), total cholesterol -0.20 mmol/L (~ -7.7 mg/dL) and LDL -0.10 mmol/L (~ -3.9 mg/dL); interventions lasted 2-24 weeks. Predicted ~13% drop in 10-year Framingham CVD risk.
claims.population: 1,917 participants across 20 randomised controlled trials of the DASH diet versus a control diet; larger BP effects in those with higher baseline BP or BMI.
claims.quote: The DASH diet was found to result in significant decreases in systolic BP ( - 5·2 mmHg, 95% CI - 7·0, - 3·4; P< 0·001) and diastolic BP ( - 2·6 mmHg, 95% CI - 3·5, - 1·7; P< 0·001) and in the concentrations of total cholesterol ( - 0·20 mmol/l, 95% CI - 0·31, - 0·10; P< 0·001) and LDL ( - 0·10 mmol/l, 95% CI - 0·20, - 0·01; P= 0·03).

claims.statement: Cutting alcohol lowers blood pressure only in people who currently drink more than two drinks a day; below that threshold, drinking less produced no measurable blood-pressure benefit.
claims.amount: In people drinking six or more standard drinks/day (12 g alcohol each) who halved their intake, systolic BP fell 5.50 mmHg (95% CI -6.70 to -4.30) and diastolic BP 3.97 mmHg (-4.70 to -3.25). At two drinks/day or fewer, no significant reduction.
claims.population: 2,865 adults (2,464 men, 401 women) in 36 trials of changed alcohol consumption lasting at least 7 days, stratified by baseline drinking level.
claims.quote: In people who drank two or fewer drinks per day, a reduction in alcohol was not associated with a significant reduction in blood pressure; however, in people who drank more than two drinks per day, a reduction in alcohol intake was associated with increased blood pressure reduction. Reduction in systolic blood pressure (mean difference -5·50 mm Hg, 95% CI -6·70 to -4·30) and diastolic blood pressure (-3·97, -4·70 to -3·25) was strongest in participants who drank six or more drinks per day if they reduced their intake by about 50%.

claims.statement: Alcohol's effect on the liver accelerates faster than linearly: doubling the daily amount roughly doubles-again the risk of cirrhosis, so the drink-count reduction matters far more at the high end.
claims.amount: Versus lifetime abstention, 25 g alcohol/day (~2 UK units, ~1.8 US drinks) carried a relative risk of 1.81 (95% CI 1.68-1.94) for cirrhosis morbidity; 50 g/day RR 3.54 (3.29-3.81); 100 g/day RR 8.15 (7.46-8.91). Mortality risks were steeper still (25 g/day RR 2.65; 100 g/day RR 16.38).
claims.population: 5,122,534 participants and 15,150 liver-cirrhosis cases pooled from 44 observational studies plus one secondary data source.
claims.quote: For morbidity, drinking 25 g/day was associated with a RR of 1.81 (95% CI 1.68-1.94) compared to lifetime abstention; 50 g/day and 100 g/day corresponded to 3.54 (95% CI 3.29-3.81) and 8.15 (95% CI 7.46-8.91), respectively. For mortality, for 25 g/day, a RR of 2.65 (95% CI 2.22-3.16); for 50 g/day, a RR of 6.83 (95% CI 5.84-7.97); for 100 g/day, a RR of 16.38 (95% CI 13.81-19.42) were identified.

claims.statement: Swapping saturated fat for polyunsaturated fat at the same total fat and calories lowers LDL by about 10 mg/dL - but the drop comes from removing the saturated fat, not from adding the polyunsaturated fat.
claims.amount: Higher polyunsaturated:saturated ratio diets (median P:S 1.2; PUFA 10.6% kcal, SFA 8.0% kcal) lowered LDL by 9.83 mg/dL (95% CI -13.63 to -6.04) vs lower-ratio diets (median P:S 0.4; SFA 12.5% kcal). Where the diets differed in SFA by >=2% of calories, LDL fell 15.72 mg/dL; where SFA was matched, only 3.45 mg/dL (non-significant).
claims.population: 1,011 generally healthy adults across 24 randomised complete-feeding trials of >=3 weeks, with diets matched for energy, fibre and total fat.
claims.quote: Higher P:S ratio diets (median P:S ratio 1.2; PUFA 10.6% kcal; SFA 8.0% kcal; and MUFA 12.6% kcal) lowered LDL cholesterol [MD -9.83 mg/dL; 95% confidence interval (CI): -13.63, -6.04; I= 79%] compared with lower P:S ratio diets (median P:S ratio 0.4; PUFA 4.4% kcal; SFA 12.5% kcal; and MUFA 14.6% kcal). Heterogeneity in the P:S ratio effect was observed by the test diet SFA content (P < 0.001). Higher compared to lower P:S ratio diets lowered LDL cholesterol (MD -15.72 mg/dL; 95% CI: -20.51, -10.92; I= 68%) when the test diets differed in SFA (≥2% kcal), but not when diets were SFA-matched (MD -3.45 mg/dL; 95% CI: -7.88, 0.98; I= 70%).

claims.statement: Reducing saturated fat for two years or more cuts cardiovascular events by about a fifth, and the trials that cut it most cut events most - but the lipid changes it produces are small, and it does not move HDL, triglycerides or blood pressure.
claims.amount: Combined cardiovascular events RR 0.79 (95% CI 0.66-0.93; 11 trials, 53,300 participants); number needed to treat 56 over ~4 years in primary prevention, 32 in secondary prevention. Little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.96, 0.90-1.03), HDL, triglycerides or blood pressure; small reductions in total cholesterol, LDL, weight and BMI.
claims.population: ~59,000 adults with or without existing cardiovascular disease in 15 randomised controlled trials of at least 24 months that reduced saturated fat versus higher saturated fat or usual diet.
claims.quote: The included long-term trials suggested that reducing dietary saturated fat reduced the risk of combined cardiovascular events by 21% (risk ratio (RR) 0.79; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.66 to 0.93, 11 trials, 53,300 participants of whom 8% had a cardiovascular event, I² = 65%, GRADE moderate-quality evidence). Meta-regression suggested that greater reductions in saturated fat (reflected in greater reductions in serum cholesterol) resulted in greater reductions in risk of CVD events, explaining most heterogeneity between trials.
claims.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

claims.statement: Industrial trans fat is the one fat that damages both sides of the lipid panel at once - it raises LDL and lowers HDL in controlled trials, unlike saturated fat which mainly raises LDL.
claims.amount: Increased trans fatty acid intake raised total cholesterol (standardised effect size 0.28, 95% CI 0.04-0.51) and LDL (0.36, 0.13-0.60) and lowered HDL (-0.25, -0.48 to -0.01). No effect on glucose, insulin or triglycerides; no dose-response detected across the trial range.
claims.population: Adults in 7 randomised, placebo-controlled trials of trans fatty acid intake reporting glucose-homeostasis and lipid outcomes.
claims.quote: Increased TFA intake led to a significant increase in total and LDL-cholesterol [ES (95% CI): 0.28 (0.04, 0.51) and 0.36 (0.13, 0.60), respectively] and a significant decrease in HDL-cholesterol concentrations [ES (95% CI): -0.25 (-0.48, -0.01)].
claims.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

claims.statement: Ultra-processed food drives overeating on its own, independent of calories, sugar, salt, fat and fibre on the label - when everything else was matched, people ate ~500 kcal/day more and gained weight in two weeks.
claims.amount: +508 +/- 106 kcal/day on the ultra-processed diet (p = 0.0001); +0.9 +/- 0.3 kg body weight over 2 weeks on ultra-processed versus -0.9 +/- 0.3 kg on unprocessed. Extra calories came from carbohydrate (+280 kcal/day) and fat (+230 kcal/day), not protein.
claims.population: 20 weight-stable adults (mean age 31.2 years, BMI 27) admitted as inpatients to the NIH Clinical Center, randomised crossover, 2 weeks per diet, meals matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fibre.
claims.quote: Energy intake was greater during the ultra-processed diet (508 ± 106 kcal/day; p = 0.0001), with increased consumption of carbohydrate (280 ± 54 kcal/day; p < 0.0001) and fat (230 ± 53 kcal/day; p = 0.0004), but not protein (-2 ± 12 kcal/day; p = 0.85). Weight changes were highly correlated with energy intake (r = 0.8, p < 0.0001), with participants gaining 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p = 0.009) during the ultra-processed diet and losing 0.9 ± 0.3 kg (p = 0.007) during the unprocessed diet.

claims.statement: In long-term population data, higher ultra-processed food intake tracks with more cardio-cerebrovascular disease and specifically more hypertension, with risk climbing steeply from the very first daily serving.
claims.amount: Highest vs lowest ultra-processed food intake: RR 1.08 (95% CI 1.01-1.16) for cardio-cerebrovascular disease. Non-linear dose-response: risk rose ~7% across an intake of up to 1 serving/day, then flattened. Subgroup analysis showed significantly increased total CVD and hypertension risk.
claims.population: 63,573,312 participants across 39 prospective cohort studies (observational, not randomised).
claims.quote: Our findings indicate a significant association between a higher consumption of UPF and an increased likelihood of CCVDs (RR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.01-1.16, I = 89%; p < 0.01) compared to individuals who either abstain from or consume lesser amounts of UPF. Nonlinear dose-response meta-analyses showed that a consistent high intake of UPFs was associated with an elevated risk of developing CCVDs (p non-linearity <0.001). Notably, the risk of CCVDs escalated by approximately 7% with an UPF intake of up to 1 serving per day. Subgroup analysis further revealed a significant augmentation in the risk of total CVD and hypertension with increased UPF consumption.
claims.journal: Nutrition, metabolism, and cardiovascular diseases : NMCD

claims.statement: Ultra-processed food intake is associated with fatty liver disease in a dose-dependent way, with the jump concentrated at the highest intakes rather than spread evenly.
claims.amount: Moderate vs low ultra-processed intake: RR 1.03 (95% CI 1.00-1.07). High vs low: RR 1.42 (1.16-1.75). Pooled across 60,961 individuals.
claims.population: 60,961 adults in 9 observational studies (3 cross-sectional, 3 case-control, 3 cohort) with NAFLD defined by steatosis scores, imaging or liver biopsy; ultra-processed intake classified with NOVA.
claims.quote: Both moderate (vs. low) (pooled relative risk 1.03 (1.00-1.07) (= 0.04) (I= 0%)) and high (vs. low) (1.42 (1.16-1.75) (<0.01) (I= 89%)) intake of UPF significantly increased the risk of NAFLD.

claims.statement: Processed red meat specifically - bacon, sausage, deli meat - shows a clean linear dose-response with fatty liver disease, so each daily portion counts rather than only heavy intakes mattering.
claims.amount: Each 25 g/day increment of processed red meat was associated with an 11.1% higher risk of NAFLD (OR 1.11, 95% CI 1.01-1.22, p = 0.029). Any red meat vs least: OR 1.27 (1.07-1.50); processed OR 1.20 (1.04-1.3); unprocessed OR 1.28 (1.05-1.55, non-linear).
claims.population: Adults in 10 observational studies of red meat consumption and NAFLD risk (authors advise caution interpreting; high heterogeneity, I-squared 81% for total red meat).
claims.quote: We also found a significant linear dose-response association between processed red meat intake and NAFLD, with each 25-g increment of processed red meat intake per day was associated with an 11.1% higher risk of NAFLD (OR = 1.11; 95% CI = 1.01-1.22, P = 0.029), and a nonlinear association between unprocessed meat intake and NAFLD (P = 0.003 for nonlinearity).

claims.statement: Sugar hurts the liver mainly when it is added on top of maintenance calories and mainly when it arrives as a drink - swapping sugar for other calories at the same energy intake did not change liver fat or liver enzymes.
claims.amount: Excess-energy ('addition') trials: standardised mean difference for intrahepatocellular lipid 1.72 (95% CI 1.08-2.36, p < 0.001) - a large effect; sugar-sweetened beverages specifically raised liver fat (high certainty) and ALT (moderate certainty). No effect in energy-matched substitution or ad libitum trials.
claims.population: 2,059 participants in 51 controlled trials (75 comparisons) of >=7 days, predominantly healthy mixed-weight or overweight/obese younger adults, across 10 food sources of fructose-containing sugars.
claims.quote: Total fructose-containing sugars increased IHCL (standardized mean difference = 1.72 [95% CI, 1.08 to 2.36], p < 0.001) in addition trials and decreased AST in subtraction trials with no effect on any outcome in substitution or ad libitum trials. There was evidence of influence by food source with SSBs increasing IHCL and ALT in addition trials and mixed sources (with SSBs) decreasing AST in subtraction trials.

claims.statement: A Mediterranean-style diet high in fibre and unsaturated fat cut liver fat by about a third in 12 weeks and improved GGT - roughly three times the liver-fat reduction of habitual diet, with only modest weight loss.
claims.amount: Liver proton-density fat fraction fell 30% on the diet without supplement and 10% in controls; weight fell 3.4 +/- 0.5 kg (4.5%) versus 1.5 +/- 0.5 kg (2.1%). Both diet groups had significantly greater reductions in weight, liver PDFF, total cholesterol, gamma-glutamyl transferase and triglycerides than controls.
claims.population: 88 Chinese women with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, randomised for 12 weeks to a culturally adapted Mediterranean-like diet (with or without C15:0 supplementation) or habitual diet.
claims.quote: In the intention-to-treat analysis, weight reductions of 4.0 ± 0.5 kg (5.3%), 3.4 ± 0.5 kg (4.5%), and 1.5 ± 0.5 kg (2.1%) were achieved in the diet-with-C15:0, diet without-C15:0, and the control groups, respectively. The proton density fat fraction (PDFF) of the liver decreased by 33%, 30%, and 10%, respectively. Both diet groups achieved significantly greater reductions in body weight, liver PDFF, total cholesterol, gamma-glutamyl transferase, and triglyceride concentrations compared with the control group.
claims.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

claims.statement: Adding oats or oat beta-glucan is one of the best-quantified single food swaps for cholesterol, cutting LDL by roughly 11 mg/dL regardless of what the rest of the diet looks like.
claims.amount: Total cholesterol -0.42 mmol/L (95% CI -0.61 to -0.22; ~ -16 mg/dL), LDL -0.29 mmol/L (-0.37 to -0.20; ~ -11 mg/dL), glucose -0.25 mmol/L, weight -0.94 kg, waist -1.06 cm. Blood-pressure and inflammation effects were not established.
claims.population: 4,937 predominantly hypercholesterolaemic or obese adults with mild metabolic disturbances across 74 randomised trials (59 in the meta-analysis) of oat, oat beta-glucan extracts or avenanthramides; 81% had some risk-of-bias concerns.
claims.quote: Subjects receiving an OSI, compared to control arms without oats, had improved levels of total cholesterol (TC) [weighted mean difference and (95% CI) - 0.42 mmol/L, (- 0.61; - 0.22)], LDL cholesterol [- 0.29 mmol/L, (- 0.37; - 0.20)], glucose [- 0.25 nmol/L, (- 0.36; - 0.14)], body mass index [- 0.13 kg/m, (- 0.26; - 0.01)], weight [- 0.94 kg, (- 1.84: - 0.05)], and waist circumference [- 1.06 cm, (- 1.85; - 0.27)].

claims.statement: Fermentable (prebiotic) fibre lowered blood pressure in people who already had hypertension, but the pooled effect vanished once people with normal blood pressure were included - the evidence base is small and mostly animal work.
claims.amount: In hypertensive cohorts, systolic BP -8.5 mmHg (95% CI -13.9 to -3.1) and diastolic BP -5.2 mmHg (-8.5 to -2.0). Pooling hypertensive plus non-hypertensive: systolic -4.5 mmHg (-9.3 to 0.3), non-significant.
claims.population: Six human interventional trials (of 19 included studies, 7 human and 12 animal) reporting post-intervention blood pressure with dietary fibre or other prebiotics; small pooled sample.
claims.quote: In hypertensive cohorts, prebiotics significantly reduced SBP (-8.5 mmHg; 95% CI: -13.9, -3.1) and DBP (-5.2 mmHg; 95% CI: -8.5, -2.0). A pooled analysis of hypertensive and non-hypertensive patients showed non-significant reductions in SBP (-4.5 mmHg; 95% CI: -9.3, 0.3) and DBP (-2.5 mmHg; 95% CI: -5.4, 0.4).

claims.statement: Long-term androgen therapy itself raises blood pressure and lowers HDL - the same two markers diet is being used to manage - and the evidence for this is observational and based on blood markers rather than measured cardiovascular damage.
claims.amount: none
claims.population: Adult transgender men on long-term gender-affirming testosterone therapy, as summarised in a narrative review of ovarian, breast and metabolic changes; findings described as mostly observational and biomarker-based.
claims.quote: Cardiometabolic risk and morbidity data are currently reassuring, even if certain studies show conflicting results. An increase in blood pressure and a decrease in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol have been reported as risk factors, whereas polycythemia is rare and treatable. Most available data are observational and based on biochemical markers instead of the more direct measures of cardiovascular damage.

claims.statement: In trained lifters, a large energy surplus (15% above maintenance) added more fat than maintenance eating without adding more muscle thickness or squat strength; across the whole sample, how fast body mass went up predicted fat gain far better than it predicted muscle growth.
claims.amount: maintenance vs 5% vs 15% energy surplus; 8 weeks; resistance training 3 d/wk; body-mass change explained 49% of variance in skinfold change vs 24% of biceps muscle-thickness change
claims.population: 21 randomised (17 completers) resistance-trained lifters of mixed training experience performing moderate training volumes 3 d/wk; sex breakdown not stated in the abstract
claims.quote: Therefore, we conclude faster rates of BM gain (and by proxy larger surpluses) primarily increase rates of fat gain rather than augmenting 1-RM or MT. However, biceps brachii, the muscle which received the greatest stimulus in this study, may have been positively impacted by greater BM gain, albeit slightly.

claims.statement: In resistance-trained men deliberately overfed for six weeks, an average body-mass gain of about 0.55% of bodyweight per week corresponded to essentially all of the gained weight being fat-free mass, but individual results scattered widely around that figure and could not be predicted in advance.
claims.amount: ~0.55% of body mass per week (target gain >=0.45 kg/week); 6 weeks of supervised resistance training plus a high-calorie protein/carbohydrate supplement
claims.population: 28 enrolled / 21 completing resistance-trained adult males; body composition by 4-component model and ultrasonography
claims.quote: On average, a BM gain of ~0.55%/week corresponded with a body composition score ((∆FFM/∆BM)*100) of 100, indicative of all BM gained as FFM. However, meaningful variability around this estimate was observed.
claims.journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology

claims.statement: The textbook sports-nutrition prescription for gaining mass (an extra 300-500 kcal/day aiming at about 0.45 kg per week, mostly lean) is not well supported by trial evidence, and that weekly rate may be unachievable for many athletes.
claims.amount: ~300-500 kcal/day extra; target ~0.45 kg (1 lb) weight gain per week
claims.population: critical review of intentional weight-gain regimens in athletes and military personnel; mixed sexes, ages and training statuses across the included literature
claims.quote: Sports nutrition guidelines typically state that athletes desiring weight gain follow a regimen that includes increasing energy intake by ~ 300-500 kcal/day ... Currently, available data suggests that weekly weight gain of 0.45 kg (1 lb), primarily as LBM, may be difficult for some athletes to achieve.

claims.statement: The most widely cited practice guidance for drug-free bodybuilders sets the off-season surplus at 10-20% above maintenance targeting 0.25-0.5% of bodyweight gained per week, and explicitly tells more advanced lifters to use a smaller surplus and slower gain.
claims.amount: 10-20% hyper-energetic diet; 0.25-0.5% of bodyweight per week; protein 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day
claims.population: narrative review written for natural (drug-free) bodybuilders in the off-season; recommendations not derived from a single study population
claims.quote: A hyper-energetic diet (~10-20%) should be consumed with a target weight gain of ~0.25-0.5% of bodyweight/week for novice/intermediate bodybuilders. Advanced bodybuilders should be more conservative with the caloric surplus and weekly weight gain.

claims.statement: No study has ever validated an optimal surplus size for maximising muscle relative to fat; the commonly quoted kcal figures come from theoretical calculations of the energy stored in new tissue, which ignore the metabolic cost of building muscle and the body's compensatory response to overfeeding.
claims.amount: none
claims.population: narrative review addressing resistance-training populations generally; no defined study sample
claims.quote: These estimates have never been validated in a resistance training population to confirm the "sweet spot" for an energy surplus that facilitates optimal rates of muscle gain relative to fat mass.

claims.statement: In elite athletes adding four strength sessions a week, eating an extra ~620 kcal/day versus eating ad libitum produced about 2.6 times more bodyweight gain, but all of the extra weight was fat: lean body mass gain did not differ between the groups.
claims.amount: 3585 +/- 601 vs 2964 +/- 884 kcal/day; 8-12 weeks; bodyweight +3.9% vs +1.5%; fat mass +15% vs +3%
claims.population: 39 elite athletes (~19 years old, both sexes) randomised to nutritional counselling (n=21) or ad libitum eating (n=18), continuing sport-specific training plus 4 strength sessions/week; DXA
claims.quote: Energy intake was higher in the NCG than in the ALG (3585+/-601 vs. 2964+/-884 kcal) and consequently BW increased more in NCG than in ALG (3.9+/-0.6% vs. 1.5+/-0.4%). Fat mass (FM) increased more in NCG than in ALG (15+/-4 vs. 3+/-3%), but gain in LBM was not different between groups.

claims.statement: A planned surplus of about 500 kcal/day plus four strength sessions a week added roughly 2.8% lean body mass over 8-12 weeks in young elite athletes, whereas athletes left to eat ad libitum gained no lean mass at all.
claims.amount: 506 +/- 84 kcal/day surplus; 8-12 weeks; LBM +2.8% during the intervention and +4.4% at 12-month follow-up; bodyweight +4.3%
claims.population: 21 young elite athletes (18.5-19.6 years, both sexes) randomised to nutritional counselling (n=12) or ad libitum intake (n=9), strength training 4 sessions/week; DXA
claims.quote: The NCG followed a meal plan that provided a surplus of 506 +/- 84 kcal.day(-1), whereas the ALG had an ad libitum energy intake (EI) during the strength-training (4 sessions per week) intervention. ... LBM increased in the NCG during the intervention (2.8% +/- 0.5%) and after 12 months (4.4% +/- 1.0%), whereas LBM in the ALG was unchanged.

claims.statement: In a 12-week bulking trial prescribing 300-500 kcal/day above requirements, the group that actually ate the full surplus gained more than twice as much fat as the group that under-ate it, while both groups gained essentially identical fat-free mass and identical strength.
claims.amount: prescribed 300-500 kcal/day surplus; 12 weeks; resistance training 3x/week; fat mass +4.36 vs +2.00 kg; fat-free mass +1.38 vs +1.34 kg
claims.population: 23 healthy resistance-trained men and women randomised to 16:8 time-restricted eating or conventional control; body composition by single-frequency bioelectrical impedance
claims.quote: Despite this, both groups showed similar increases in fat-free mass (TRE: +1.34 ± 0.78; CON: +1.38 ± 1.42 kg) and muscle mass (+1.07 ± 0.94; +1.13 ± 0.61 kg). The CON group showed significantly greater increases in BW (+2.19 ± 2.40; +3.90 ± 2.14 kg; P = 0.018) and fat mass (+2.00 ± 2.49; +4.36 ± 2.26 kg; P = 0.009).

claims.statement: A modest single-digit surplus is enough to support substantial lean gains in already well-trained lifters: 10% above maintenance with 2.2 g/kg/day protein produced 1.8-2.7 kg of fat-free mass in 8 weeks, and the arm that accumulated more fat gained no more fat-free mass for it.
claims.amount: 10% hypercaloric; protein 2.2 g/kg/day; 8 weeks; resistance exercise 4x/week; fat-free mass +2.67 kg (TRE) and +1.82 kg (control)

claims.quote: When comparing within groups, five days of low EA (15kcal·kgLBM·d) decreased bone formation and increased bone resorption in women, but not in men, and no sex specific differences were detected.
