claims.population: 160 adults with obesity or overweight from SURMOUNT-1 (124 pooled tirzepatide, 36 placebo), 73% female, mean weight 102.5 kg, mean BMI 38.0 kg/m2
claims.quote: The change in body weight, fat mass and lean mass from baseline to Week 72 was -21.3%, -33.9% and -10.9% with tirzepatide and -5.3%, -8.2% and -2.6% with placebo, respectively (p < 0.001 for all comparisons). Of the body weight lost, approximately 75% was fat mass and 25% was lean mass for both tirzepatide and placebo.

claims.statement: Pooling 22 trials, GLP-1 drugs cut lean mass by just under a kilogram on average (about a quarter of total weight lost), but lean mass as a percentage of body weight did not fall - the drugs that produced the most weight loss preserved lean mass least.
claims.amount: lean mass -0.86 kg (95% CI -1.30 to -0.42); total weight -3.55 kg; fat mass -2.95 kg; lean loss ~25% of total; relative lean mass unchanged
claims.population: 2,258 adults with diabetes and/or overweight/obesity across 22 RCTs of GLP-1 RAs and GLP-1/GIP dual agonists
claims.quote: GLP-1RAs significantly reduced total body weight (MD -3.55 kg, 95 %-CI [-4.81, -2.29]), fat mass (MD -2.95 kg, 95 %-CI [-4.11, -1.79]), and lean mass (MD -0.86 kg, 95 %-CI [-1.30, -0.42]), with lean mass loss comprising approximately 25 % of the total weight loss. However, the relative lean mass, defined as percentage change from baseline, was unaffected. ... Tirzepatide (15 mg weekly) and semaglutide (2.4 mg weekly) were the most effective for weight and fat mass reduction but were among the least effective in preserving lean mass.

claims.statement: Measured by MRI rather than DXA, thigh muscle volume fell on tirzepatide by about the amount expected for that much weight loss in the general population - and fat infiltrating the muscle actually decreased more than expected, suggesting muscle quality improved.
claims.amount: thigh muscle volume -0.64 L (95% CI -0.74 to -0.54); muscle fat infiltration -0.36 percentage points; muscle volume vs population-based estimate -0.04 L (p=0.22, i.e. no excess loss); 52 weeks
claims.population: 246 insulin-naive adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin with or without an SGLT-2 inhibitor (mean age 56.0 y, mean BMI 33.4 kg/m2, 59.8% male), randomized to tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg or insulin degludec, SURPASS-3 MRI substudy
claims.quote: In tirzepatide-treated participants, observed muscle volume changes across all tirzepatide doses were similar to population-based estimated changes (for pooled tirzepatide, mean difference vs population-based estimate, -0.04 L [95% CI -0.11 to 0.03], p=0.22); whereas, observed reductions in muscle fat infiltration across all doses were significantly greater than population-based estimates (for pooled tirzepatide, mean difference -0.42 percentage points [95% CI -0.54 to -0.31], p<0.0001)

claims.statement: Framed against ageing, the muscle loss in the pivotal obesity trials is large: participants lost 10% or more of their muscle mass in under 18 months, roughly what two decades of ageing would cost.
claims.amount: 10% or more of muscle mass over 68-72 weeks; approximately equivalent to 20 years of age-related muscle loss
claims.population: Clinical trial participants with obesity receiving incretin-mimetic drugs (principally semaglutide and tirzepatide) in 68-72 week interventions
claims.quote: Available evidence suggests that clinical trial participants receiving IMDs for the treatment of obesity lost 10% or more of their muscle mass during the 68- to 72-week interventions, approximately equivalent to 20 years of age-related muscle loss. The ability to maintain muscle mass during caloric restriction-induced weight reduction is influenced by two key factors: nutrition and physical exercise.

claims.statement: Incretin drugs strip roughly 6 kg of lean mass, while supervised resistance training programs longer than 10 weeks independently add about 3 kg of lean mass and 25% strength - the arithmetic behind recommending lifting alongside these drugs.
claims.amount: lean mass loss ~10% or ~6 kg with 15-24% total weight loss; resistance training >10 weeks: lean mass +~3 kg, strength +~25%
claims.population: Adults with overweight and obesity in randomized trials of liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide; resistance-training effect sizes drawn from supervised training trials in men and women
claims.quote: However, these agents also cause rapid and significant loss of lean mass (~10% or ~6 kg), comparable to a decade or more of aging. ... Studies indicate that supervised resistance exercise training interventions with a duration >10 weeks can elicit large increases in lean mass (~3 kg) and strength (~25%) in men and women.

claims.statement: The most explicit published protein prescription for GLP-1 users is at least 1.2 g/kg/day, up to 1.6 g/kg in people without kidney disease, split into per-meal doses of 0.3-0.4 g/kg containing about 2.5-3 g of leucine - a proposed framework, not a tested one.
claims.amount: protein 1.2 g/kg/day minimum, up to 1.6 g/kg/day; ~0.3-0.4 g/kg per meal; ~2.5-3 g leucine per meal; lab panel of vitamin D, B12, iron studies, folate, zinc, thiamine
claims.population: Adults with obesity on GLP-1 RA or GIP/GLP-1 therapy; narrative review proposing a dietitian-led framework with adaptations for older adults, type 2 diabetes, CKD, vegetarian/vegan and sarcopenic obesity. Not validated in any trial.
claims.quote: We propose pragmatic energy floors to preserve micronutrient adequacy; daily protein intakes of >=1.2 g/kg (up to 1.6 g/kg in appropriate adults without chronic kidney disease (CKD)) with meal-wise targets of ~0.3-0.4 g/kg and ~2.5-3 g leucine; a structured laboratory panel (vitamin D, B12, iron studies, folate, zinc, and thiamine in high-risk patients); and integration of progressive resistance training.

claims.statement: The first randomized trial designed to test whether protein and lifting actually preserve muscle on semaglutide or tirzepatide is still running - only its protocol has been published, so the central practical question has no trial answer yet.
claims.amount: 232 adults; 1.6 g/kg/day protein target; 3 home resistance sessions/week progressing 1 to 3 sets; 6 months; primary outcome MRI quadriceps cross-sectional area
claims.population: 232 adults with obesity in Kuwait initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide, randomized 1:1:1:1 to control, resistance exercise, protein supplementation, or both combined (NCT06885736). Results not yet reported.
claims.quote: This single-centre, 6-month, randomised controlled trial at Dasman Diabetes Institute will enrol 232 adults with obesity, randomised (1:1:1:1) to control, resistance exercise, protein supplementation or combined resistance exercise and protein in conjunction with semaglutide or tirzepatide therapy. Resistance exercise will be home-based and involve three sessions per week, progressing from one to three sets targeting major muscle groups. Protein supplementation will target 1.6 g/kg/day via dietary adjustment and protein products.

claims.statement: In a real-world cohort given no nutrition support, people who ate more total protein retained more muscle - the closest thing to direct human evidence that protein intake matters on these drugs, and it is a weak correlation in 28 people.
claims.amount: r = 0.41, P = 0.0498 for absolute protein intake vs preservation of estimated skeletal muscle mass; ~one quarter of weight loss was estimated skeletal muscle mass; n = 28 over 24 weeks
claims.population: 28 adults with obesity initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide in a real-world clinic, followed 24 weeks with no structured nutrition intervention; body composition by bioelectrical impedance analysis (CRAVE study, NCT06467604)
claims.quote: GLP-1 RA OMM therapy was associated with significant reductions in body weight, adiposity, and BIA-estimated skeletal muscle mass (all P < 0.001); with approximately one-quarter of weight loss attributable to estimated skeletal muscle mass. Total energy intake decreased significantly, with parallel reductions in macronutrient intake. Higher absolute protein intake was associated with greater preservation of estimated skeletal muscle mass (r = 0.41, P = 0.0498).

claims.statement: In the same cohort, diet quality did not improve and intake of multiple micronutrients fell significantly - appetite suppression shrinks the whole plate rather than trimming the junk off it.
claims.amount: 24 weeks; n = 28; significant declines across multiple micronutrients; Healthy Eating Index (HEI-2020) unchanged; food cravings unchanged overall
claims.population: 28 adults with obesity initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide in a real-world clinic without structured nutrition support, 24 weeks (CRAVE study)
claims.quote: Diet quality did not significantly improve in our sample and food cravings were unchanged overall, although higher baseline cravings were associated with greater reductions over time (r = -0.69, P < 0.001). Significant declines in intake were observed across multiple micronutrients.

claims.statement: Protein holds its share of the diet on GLP-1 therapy (about 14-17.5% of calories), but because total calories collapse, absolute grams of protein can fall below the threshold needed to trigger muscle protein synthesis.
claims.amount: protein maintained at approximately 13.9-17.5% of total energy intake in liraglutide trials
claims.population: Older adults with type 2 diabetes and/or obesity on GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists; review of randomized trials reporting dietary protein intake
claims.quote: Randomized trials suggest that liraglutide generally maintains protein intake as a proportion of total energy (approximately 13.9-17.5%), yet reductions in absolute protein intake may occur due to overall caloric restriction, particularly with more potent appetite suppression. Importantly, even when proportional intake is preserved, reductions in total energy intake may lower absolute protein consumption below levels required to adequately stimulate muscle protein synthesis in older adults.

claims.statement: Semaglutide 2.4 mg cuts intake at a free-choice meal by about a third - the mechanism that makes protein targets hard to hit. Notably this trial found no delayed gastric emptying at 20 weeks by paracetamol absorption, an indirect method, even though delayed emptying is the usual explanation for the GI symptoms.
claims.amount: ad libitum energy intake 35% lower than placebo (1736 vs 2676 kJ; treatment difference -940 kJ, P<0.0001); body weight -9.9% vs -0.4%; 20 weeks
claims.population: 72 adults with obesity randomized to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide escalated to 2.4 mg or placebo for 20 weeks
claims.quote: Ad libitum energy intake was 35% lower with semaglutide versus placebo (1736 versus 2676 kJ; estimated treatment difference -940 kJ; P <0.0001). Semaglutide reduced hunger and prospective food consumption, and increased fullness and satiety when compared with placebo (all P <0.02). ... There was no evidence of delayed gastric emptying at week 20, assessed indirectly via paracetamol absorption.

claims.statement: Across studies that measured it, GLP-1 and dual agonists cut total daily calorie intake by 16-39% - but hardly any study recorded what the remaining diet was actually made of.
claims.amount: total caloric intake reduced by 16-39%
claims.population: Adults with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes using GLP-1 RAs or dual GIP/GLP-1 RAs; narrative review of clinical studies quantifying dietary intake
claims.quote: Though data from these studies reveal that total caloric intake was reduced by 16-39 %, few studies evaluated the actual composition of the diet. ... Further research is needed to understand the unique nutritional needs of adults on GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1RAs and to support the development of nutritional guidelines for these individuals.

claims.statement: 40-70% of patients get gastrointestinal side effects, and the recommended first response is dietary rather than pharmacological: smaller and more frequent meals, adequate hydration, and avoiding high-fat and high-sugar foods.
claims.amount: 40% to 70% incidence of GI adverse effects; dietary first-line: smaller more frequent meals, adequate hydration, avoidance of high-fat or high-sugar foods; 24-hour liquid diet before endoscopy in high-risk patients
claims.population: Patients with type 2 diabetes or obesity on GLP-1 RAs or dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists in primary care; clinical management review, dietary advice is expert recommendation rather than trial-derived
claims.quote: However, 40% to 70% of patients experience gastrointestinal adverse effects, such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, delayed gastric emptying, and biliary disease. High-quality studies have not yet confirmed an increased risk of pancreatitis. Management of gastrointestinal symptoms should start with dietary modifications-smaller, more frequent meals; adequate hydration; and avoidance of high-fat or high-sugar foods.

claims.statement: A systematic review of 16 randomized trials found GI symptoms occurred despite background dietary counselling, lean mass was broadly preserved in proportion to weight loss, and no trial has established what the optimal diet actually is.
claims.amount: 16 trials, 7,096 participants; no study assessed bone health; none reported clinically relevant nutritional deficiencies
claims.population: 7,096 adults with obesity, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes receiving GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists alongside lifestyle or dietary guidance, across 16 RCTs (PROSPERO CRD420251181076)
claims.quote: GLP-1 and dual agonists consistently increased gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, diarrhoea, constipation and vomiting. These effects were often dose-related and occurred despite background lifestyle or dietary interventions. Lean mass was generally preserved, with reductions proportional to overall weight loss. No study directly assessed bone health, and none reported clinically relevant nutritional deficiencies. ... Although dietary guidance is commonly provided, evidence on optimal nutritional approaches remains limited. Further trials are needed to clarify protein requirements, assess musculoskeletal outcomes and establish evidence-based dietary recommendations

claims.statement: Dietary fiber is proposed to ease GLP-1-related constipation and stabilise the gut microbiome, but raising intake too quickly causes bloating and gas, and no trial has yet tested fiber alongside a GLP-1 drug.
claims.amount: none
claims.population: Adults with obesity on GLP-1 receptor agonists; mechanistic and narrative review of fiber-GLP-1 interactions. No completed trial combining a characterized fiber with a GLP-1 RA.
claims.quote: Tolerability can be limited by bloating or gas, particularly if intake is increased too rapidly. ... We explore opportunities for fibers to mitigate GLP-1RA-related adverse effects, support bowel regularity, and stabilize the microbiota during treatment or after discontinuation. ... Well-designed trials that combine GLP-1RAs with well-characterized fibers, include microbiome endpoints, and assess long-term outcomes are needed to optimize efficacy and reduce dependence on costly pharmacotherapy.

claims.statement: Adding a supervised exercise program to liraglutide roughly doubled the fall in body-fat percentage versus either alone - the strongest randomized evidence that training changes the composition, not just the amount, of GLP-1 weight loss.
claims.amount: body fat: combination -3.9 percentage points vs exercise -1.7 and liraglutide -1.9; weight -9.5 kg vs placebo; liraglutide 3.0 mg/day; 52 weeks after an 8-week low-calorie diet
claims.population: 195 adults with obesity (BMI 32-43) without diabetes, mean 13.1 kg lost on an 8-week low-calorie diet, then randomized 1 year to exercise+placebo, liraglutide 3.0 mg, both combined, or placebo
claims.quote: The combination strategy decreased body-fat percentage by 3.9 percentage points, which was approximately twice the decrease in the exercise group (-1.7 percentage points; 95% CI, -3.2 to -0.2; P = 0.02) and the liraglutide group (-1.9 percentage points; 95% CI, -3.3 to -0.5; P = 0.009). Only the combination strategy was associated with improvements in the glycated hemoglobin level, insulin sensitivity, and cardiorespiratory fitness.

claims.statement: In that same trial, strength relative to body weight improved on exercise, liraglutide or both while falling ~8% on placebo - because absolute strength was preserved even as weight came off. Liraglutide alone did not improve any measure of physical fitness.
claims.amount: relative muscle strength over 52 weeks: placebo -7.8%, exercise -0.4%, liraglutide +1.0%, combination +3.3%; combination improved stair-climb time by 1.2 s (8.6%) and peak VO2 by 3.0 mL/min/kg fat-free mass vs liraglutide alone
claims.population: 193 adults with obesity (BMI 32-43, age 18-65) without diabetes; secondary analysis; strength measured as isometric knee extensor peak torque
claims.quote: Compared with placebo (- 7.8%), relative muscle strength (strength normalized to body weight) was higher with exercise (- 0.4%), liraglutide (+ 1.0%), and the combined treatment (+ 3.3%) because of lower weight and preserved absolute strength. ... Exercise alone led to similar benefits, whereas liraglutide alone did not improve physical fitness.

claims.statement: A year after all treatment stopped, people who had exercised held their weight loss while those who had only taken liraglutide regained 6 kg more - training buys durability that the drug alone does not.
claims.amount: weight regain 6.0 kg (95% CI 2.1-10.0) larger after stopping liraglutide than after stopping supervised exercise, weeks 52-104; odds of maintaining >=10% loss 4.2x higher for prior combination vs prior liraglutide
claims.population: 109 of 195 adults with obesity from the Copenhagen liraglutide/exercise trial, assessed one year after all treatment ended (week 104)
claims.quote: During the year after termination of treatment (week 52-104), weight regain was 6.0 kg [2.1; 10.0] larger after termination of liraglutide compared with after termination of supervised exercise and 2.5 kg [-1.5 to 6.5] compared with after termination of combination treatment.

claims.statement: Grip strength is generally preserved short-term despite lean-tissue loss, and in young men tirzepatide added to resistance and aerobic training gave no strength benefit beyond training alone - but longer-term data in older adults with diabetes show grip strength declining.
claims.amount: none
claims.population: Adults with obesity in short-to-mid-term semaglutide or liraglutide trials; young men on tirzepatide combined with resistance and aerobic training; older adults with type 2 diabetes in longitudinal and retrospective studies of prolonged semaglutide use
claims.quote: Short-to-mid-term trials of semaglutide or liraglutide in adults with obesity have shown statistically preserved handgrip strength despite reductions in lean soft tissue mass, suggesting that muscle strength may not decline proportionally to weight loss. Likewise, tirzepatide combined with resistance and aerobic training in young men may not confer additional strength benefits beyond exercise alone. In contrast, longitudinal and retrospective research in older adults with type 2 diabetes have reported reductions in handgrip strength and accelerated sarcopenia with prolonged semaglutide use

claims.statement: Four US professional societies jointly name GI side-effect management, protein adequacy, micronutrient sufficiency and resistance training as the core nutritional priorities during GLP-1 therapy - while conceding this kind of care is not yet widespread.
claims.amount: GLP-1s reduce body weight by 5% to 18% in trials, with modestly lower effects in real-world analyses
claims.population: Adults with obesity treated with GLP-1 RAs and combination incretin medications; expert-group advisory from the American College of Lifestyle Medicine, American Society for Nutrition, Obesity Medicine Association and The Obesity Society
claims.quote: During GLP-1 use, nutritional and medical management of gastrointestinal side effects is critical, as is navigating altered dietary preferences and intakes, preventing nutrient deficiencies, preserving muscle and bone mass through resistance training and appropriate diet, and complementary lifestyle interventions. ... Numerous practice guidelines recommend multicomponent, evidence-based nutritional and behavioral therapy for adults with obesity, but use of such therapies with GLP-1s is not widespread.

claims.statement: The FDA label for semaglutide sets no macronutrient or protein target at all - it only requires the drug be used together with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity, and lists GI symptoms as the most common adverse reactions.
claims.amount: initiate 0.25 mg once weekly for 4 weeks, titrate every 4 weeks; adult maintenance 2.4 mg (recommended) or 1.7 mg once weekly
claims.population: Adults and pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with obesity, and adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related comorbid condition (US prescribing information, WEGOVY)
claims.quote: WEGOVY is indicated in combination with a reduced calorie diet and increased physical activity ... Administer WEGOVY in combination with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. ... Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5%) in adults or pediatric patients aged 12 years and older are: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, headache, fatigue, dyspepsia, dizziness, abdominal distension, eructation, hypoglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes, flatulence, gastroenteritis, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and nasopharyngitis
claims.journal: FDA US Prescribing Information via DailyMed (Novo Nordisk)

claims.statement: Tirzepatide's label makes slow dose escalation - not diet - its stated tool for limiting GI side effects, and like semaglutide specifies only a reduced-calorie diet with no protein or macronutrient guidance.
claims.amount: start 2.5 mg subcutaneously once weekly for 4 weeks, increase in 2.5 mg increments after at least 4 weeks; maintenance 5, 10 or 15 mg weekly; maximum 15 mg weekly
claims.population: Adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related comorbid condition; and adults with obesity and moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (US prescribing information, ZEPBOUND)
claims.quote: ZEPBOUND is indicated in combination with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity ... The recommended starting dosage of ZEPBOUND for all indications is 2.5 mg injected subcutaneously once weekly for 4 weeks. ... Follow the dosage escalation below for all indications to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal adverse reactions ... The most common adverse reactions, reported in >=5% of patients treated with ZEPBOUND are: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain, dyspepsia, injection site reactions, fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, eructation, hair loss, gastroesophageal reflux disease.
claims.journal: FDA US Prescribing Information via DailyMed (Eli Lilly and Company)

claims.statement: Behavioural weight-loss programmes that use smartphone or other mobile self-monitoring of diet and activity produce moderately greater weight loss AND higher adherence than the same programmes using paper diaries or usual care, with the effect most pronounced in the first six months.
claims.amount: 20 pooled studies; adherence advantage over paper recording persisted at 6 and 12 months
claims.population: Adults with overweight or obesity enrolled in behavioural weight-management interventions, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies
claims.quote: Twenty studies were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis, yielding a moderate decrease in weight and higher adherence to intervention of behavioral weight management interventions using lifestyle mHealth self-monitoring, which was greater than other interventions.

claims.statement: Across four popular diets with very different structures, how much weight someone lost tracked how well they adhered, not which diet they were assigned to; overall adherence was low in every arm and only 50-65% of people completed the year.
claims.amount: 1 year; mean weight loss 2.1-3.3 kg across Atkins, Zone, Weight Watchers and Ornish
claims.population: 160 overweight or obese US adults aged 22-72 with hypertension, dyslipidaemia or fasting hyperglycaemia, randomised to one of four popular diets for 12 months
claims.quote: Amount of weight loss was associated with self-reported dietary adherence level (r = 0.60; P<.001) but not with diet type (r = 0.07; P = .40).

claims.statement: When people record their own intake they systematically under-report it against objectively measured energy expenditure, and the size of the error varies with body size, dietary restraint and socioeconomic status - so a food log is primarily a behaviour-change tool, not a measurement instrument.
claims.amount: none
claims.population: Review of doubly-labelled-water validation studies spanning adults, children and adolescents, people with obesity, athletes, military personnel and trekking explorers
claims.quote: However, in instances where the subjects themselves report their intake, EI is generally under-reported when compared with energy expenditure.

claims.statement: The per-meal protein dose that maximally stimulates muscle protein synthesis scales with body size rather than being a fixed number of grams: roughly 0.24 g per kg of body mass in young men and about 0.40 g per kg in older men.
claims.amount: 0.24 +/- 0.06 g/kg body mass (young) vs 0.40 +/- 0.19 g/kg body mass (older); 0.25 vs 0.60 g/kg lean body mass
claims.population: Healthy older (~71 y) and younger (~22 y) men given single boluses of 0-40 g high-quality protein, retrospectively pooled across laboratory infusion studies
claims.quote: Biphase linear regression and breakpoint analysis revealed the slope of first line segment was lower (p < .05) in older men and that MPS reached a plateau after ingestion of 0.40 ± 0.19 and 0.24 ± 0.06 g/kg body mass (p = .055) and 0.60 ± 0.29 and 0.25 ± 0.13 g/kg lean body mass (p < .01) in older and younger men, respectively.
claims.journal: The Journals of Gerontology. Series A, Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences

claims.statement: Leucine content, not just total grams of protein, drives the acute muscle-building signal: a small 6.25 g whey dose fortified to 5.0 g total leucine stimulated muscle protein synthesis about as well as 25 g of whey (which itself supplies 3.0 g leucine).
claims.amount: 6.25 g whey (0.75 g leucine) fortified to 3.0 g or 5.0 g total leucine, vs 25 g whey (3.0 g leucine)
claims.population: 40 healthy young men (21 +/- 1 y) after unilateral knee-extensor resistance exercise, double-blind randomised parallel-group design with muscle biopsies
claims.quote: A low-protein (6.25 g) mixed macronutrient beverage can be as effective as a high-protein dose (25 g) at stimulating increased MPS rates when supplemented with a high (5.0 g total leucine) amount of leucine.
claims.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition

claims.statement: Plant proteins generally trigger a smaller acute muscle protein synthesis response than animal proteins, mainly because of lower digestibility, greater splanchnic extraction and a lower essential-amino-acid and leucine content - a gap that can be closed by eating a larger dose, blending sources, or fortifying with the limiting amino acid.
claims.amount: none
claims.population: Narrative review of human postprandial muscle protein synthesis studies comparing plant-derived proteins (mainly soy and wheat) with animal-derived proteins
claims.quote: The proposed lower anabolic properties of plant- versus animal-derived proteins may be compensated for by (i) consuming a greater amount of the plant-derived protein or plant-based protein source to compensate for the lesser quality; (ii) using specific blends of plant-based proteins to create a more balanced amino acid profile; (iii) fortifying the plant-based protein (source) with the specific free amino acid(s) that is (are) deficient.

claims.statement: When total protein is held at 1.6 g per kg per day, protein source stops mattering for training outcomes: over 12 weeks of supervised resistance training an exclusively plant-based diet produced the same gains in leg lean mass, muscle cross-sectional area, fibre size and leg-press strength as a protein-matched mixed diet.
claims.amount: 1.6 g protein/kg body mass/day for 12 weeks, twice-weekly supervised resistance training
claims.population: 19 young men who were habitual vegans and 19 omnivores (~26 y, previously untrained); groups were defined by habitual diet rather than randomised, with supplemental soy or whey used to match intake
claims.quote: A high-protein (~ 1.6 g kg day), exclusively plant-based diet (plant-based whole foods + soy protein isolate supplementation) is not different than a protein-matched mixed diet (mixed whole foods + whey protein supplementation) in supporting muscle strength and mass accrual, suggesting that protein source does not affect resistance training-induced adaptations in untrained young men consuming adequate amounts of protein.

claims.statement: Energy density and portion size raise intake independently and additively, and the two stack: the biggest portion of the more energy-dense entree drove 56% more energy intake than the smallest portion of the less energy-dense one.
claims.amount: entrees of 5.23 vs 7.32 kJ/g (about 1.25 vs 1.75 kcal/g), each served at 500, 700 or 900 g
claims.population: 39 women served ad libitum breakfast, lunch and dinner one day a week for 6 weeks in a within-subjects crossover design
claims.quote: Increases in portion size and energy density led to independent and additive increases in energy intake (P <0.0001). Subjects consumed 56% more energy (925 kJ) when served the largest portion of the higher energy-dense entrée than when served the smallest portion of the lower energy-dense entrée.
claims.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition

claims.statement: In a real behavioural trial, the third of participants who cut their diet's energy density the most lost 5.9 kg versus 2.4 kg in the third who cut it least - and they did it while eating about 300 g MORE food per day, i.e. larger meals for fewer calories.
claims.amount: highest vs lowest tertile of energy-density reduction over 6 months: -5.9 kg vs -2.4 kg; +300 g/d vs -100 g/d food weight; -500 vs ~0 kcal/d
claims.population: 658 prehypertensive and hypertensive adults with overweight or obesity randomised to behavioural interventions in the PREMIER trial, with two 24-hour dietary recalls
claims.quote: When groups were combined and analyzed by ED change tertiles, participants in the highest tertile (ie, largest ED reduction) lost more weight (5.9 kg) than did those in the middle (4.0 kg) or lowest (2.4 kg) tertile. Participants in the highest and middle tertiles increased the weight of food they consumed (300 and 80 g/d, respectively) but decreased their EI (500 and 250 kcal/d).
claims.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition

claims.statement: For the tempting foods people find hardest to control, portioning beats banning: over a year, women who more often ate a limited portion of a problem food lost weight faster, while the three avoidance strategies were used frequently but showed no relationship to weight loss at all.
claims.amount: 1-year randomised trial; 8 behavioural strategies rated at months 0, 6 and 12
claims.population: 186 women with overweight and obesity in a one-year randomised weight-loss trial comparing eat-less advice, energy-density-based portions and pre-portioned foods
claims.quote: The three avoidance strategies for problem foods were reported to be frequently used but were not found to be related to weight loss. These results suggest that adopting and maintaining strategies to manage portions of problem foods, rather than avoiding exposure to them, can be a more useful approach for weight loss.

claims.statement: How food is processed changes how much of it people eat even when the numbers on the plan are identical: with meals matched for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fibre, participants ate about 508 kcal/day more on the ultra-processed menu and gained ~0.9 kg in two weeks, versus losing ~0.9 kg on the unprocessed menu.
claims.amount: +508 +/- 106 kcal/day; +0.9 kg vs -0.9 kg body weight over 2 weeks per arm
claims.population: 20 weight-stable adults (mean 31 y, BMI ~27) living as inpatients at the NIH Clinical Center, randomised crossover, 2 weeks on each diet, eating ad libitum
claims.quote: Energy intake was greater during the ultra-processed diet (508 ± 106 kcal/day; p = 0.0001), with increased consumption of carbohydrate (280 ± 54 kcal/day; p < 0.0001) and fat (230 ± 53 kcal/day; p = 0.0004), but not protein (-2 ± 12 kcal/day; p = 0.85).

claims.statement: Soluble fibres are not interchangeable for appetite control: pooled effects on post-meal energy intake were largest for guar gum and smallest for pectin, with the doses that worked being around 5 g (guar gum in a milk drink), 5-9 g (alginate) and 25 g (polydextrose). The review's own authors rated every included trial as high risk of bias.
claims.amount: guar gum 5 g; alginate 5 g in liquid or 9 g in solid meals; polydextrose 25 g; pooled effect sizes -0.90 (guar gum), -0.44 (beta-glucan), -0.42 (alginate), -0.36 (polydextrose), -0.26 (pectin)
claims.population: Healthy adults in randomised controlled trials of soluble dietary fibre, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims.quote: Meta-analysis of statistically pooled data for guar gum showed a sizeable effect on post-meal energy intake, followed by β-glucan, alginate, polydextrose and pectin, with pooled effect sizes of -0.90, -0.44, -0.42, -0.36 and -0.26, respectively.

claims.statement: Adding fibre is a much less reliable fullness lever than it is usually sold as: across 107 acute treatments only 39% significantly reduced subjective appetite and only 22% reduced food or energy intake, and neither the type nor the dose of fibre predicted which ones worked.
claims.amount: 107 treatments from 44 publications, 38 different fibre sources, treatment periods of 24 hours or less
claims.population: Healthy human participants in 44 published acute fibre-feeding studies measuring appetite and food or energy intake
claims.quote: The percentage of treatments that significantly reduced subjective appetite rating compared with the control was 39%. The percentage that significantly reduced food or energy intake was 22%.
claims.journal: Journal of the American College of Nutrition

claims.statement: A deliberately simplified plan can be nearly as effective as a complex one: being told only to eat more fibre produced 2.1 kg of weight loss at 12 months versus 2.7 kg for the full multicomponent American Heart Association diet, with similar dropout in both arms (9.9% vs 12.6%).
claims.amount: 12 months; -2.1 kg (fibre-only goal) vs -2.7 kg (AHA multicomponent); between-group difference 0.6 kg (95% CI -0.5 to 1.7)
claims.population: 240 adults with the metabolic syndrome in Worcester, Massachusetts, randomised to a single-component high-fibre goal or the multicomponent AHA diet with individual and group sessions
claims.quote: The more complex AHA diet may result in up to 1.7 kg more weight loss; however, a simplified approach to weight reduction emphasizing only increased fiber intake may be a reasonable alternative for persons with difficulty adhering to more complicated diet regimens.

claims.statement: Planning meals ahead is associated with a more varied, more guideline-adherent diet and lower odds of obesity - 57% of a very large French cohort planned at least occasionally - but the analysis is cross-sectional and cannot establish that planning causes the better outcomes.
claims.amount: 40,554 participants; odds of obesity 0.79 (95% CI 0.73-0.86) in women and 0.81 (0.69-0.94) in men; odds of top-quartile food variety 1.25 (1.18-1.32)
claims.population: 40,554 French adults in the web-based observational NutriNet-Sante cohort, cross-sectional analysis with repeated 24-hour dietary records and self-reported height and weight
claims.quote: In women, meal planning was associated with lower odds of being overweight (OR = 0.92 [0.87-0.98]) and obese (OR = 0.79 [0.73-0.86]). In men, the association was significant for obesity only (OR = 0.81 [0.69-0.94]).
claims.journal: International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity

claims.statement: Splitting a diet into two-week blocks of restriction alternating with two-week blocks of eating at maintenance produced substantially more weight and fat loss than the same restriction run continuously, for the same total 16 weeks of actual restriction, and blunted the drop in resting energy expenditure.
claims.amount: 8 x 2-week blocks at 67% of maintenance energy needs alternating with 7 x 2-week blocks at energy balance (30 weeks total) vs 16 weeks continuous at 67%
claims.population: 51 men with obesity (mean ~39 y, ~110 kg, BMI ~34) randomised to continuous or intermittent energy restriction; 36 completed per protocol
claims.quote: For the N=19 CON and N=17 INT who completed the intervention per protocol, weight loss was greater for INT (14.1±5.6 vs 9.1±2.9 kg; P<0.001). INT had greater FM loss (12.3±4.8 vs 8.0±4.2 kg; P<0.01), but FFM loss was similar (INT: 1.8±1.6 vs CON: 1.2±2.5 kg; P=0.4).

claims.statement: In resistance-trained adults, that same intermittent structure did NOT improve fat loss or fat-free-mass retention over 12 weeks of restriction - fat mass, fat-free mass, strength, endurance, resting energy expenditure and hormones were all comparable - but it did reduce hunger and desire to eat and raise satisfaction, which is an adherence benefit rather than a physiological one.
claims.amount: 4 x 3-week blocks of moderate restriction with 3 x 1-week energy-balance blocks (15 weeks elapsed) vs 12 weeks of continuous moderate restriction
claims.population: 61 resistance-trained adults (32 women), mean age 28.7 y, 77.2 kg, 25.5% body fat, randomised, intention-to-treat analysis (ICECAP trial)
claims.quote: Similar fat loss and fat-free mass retention are achieved with mIER and mCER during 12 wk of energy restriction; however, mIER is associated with reduced appetite.
claims.journal: Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise

claims.statement: A single one-week diet break at estimated maintenance calories, taken after 12 weeks of dieting, lowered hunger, desire to eat and irritability and raised fullness, satisfaction and alertness, alongside small increases in body weight (0.6 kg), fat-free mass (0.7 kg), resting energy expenditure and leg muscle endurance, with no change in fat mass or strength.
claims.amount: 1 week at predicted weight-maintenance energy intake (carbohydrate-led); +0.6 kg body weight, +0.7 kg fat-free mass, resting energy expenditure 7000 to 7200 kJ/day
claims.population: 26 resistance-trained athletes (42% female, mean 29.3 y, 72.7 kg, 21.3% body fat) who had just completed 12 weeks of intermittent energy restriction; pre-specified but uncontrolled pre-post secondary analysis
claims.quote: Participants reported significantly lower sensations of hunger (P = 0.017), prospective consumption (P = 0.020) and irritability (P = 0.041) after the diet break, and significantly higher sensations of fullness (P = 0.002), satisfaction (P = 0.002), and alertness (P = 0.003).

claims.statement: A two-consecutive-day weekly higher-carbohydrate refeed inside a roughly 25% deficit produced the same body-weight and fat loss as continuous restriction over 7 weeks; the trial's authors reported better retention of fat-free mass and resting metabolic rate with the refeed.
claims.amount: ~25% caloric restriction for 7 weeks with 4 resistance-training days/week; 2 consecutive elevated-carbohydrate days followed by 5 restricted days each week
claims.population: 27 resistance-trained men and women (25 +/- 6.1 y, 80 +/- 15.6 kg) randomised to a weekly refeed group (n=13) or continuous restriction (n=14)
claims.quote: A 2-day carbohydrate refeed preserves FFM, dryFFM, and RMR during energy restriction compared to continuous energy restriction in RT-individuals.
claims.journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology

claims.statement: That refeed result should be treated as unresolved: an independent reanalysis published as a formal comment concluded that only dry fat-free mass actually differed between the refeed and continuous groups, contrary to the original paper's stated conclusions about fat-free mass and resting metabolic rate. (The comment's abstract is a stub in PubMed, so the finding is quoted from its full title.)
claims.amount: none
claims.population: Independent statistical reanalysis by five authors of the 27 resistance-trained adults in the Campbell et al. weekly-refeed randomised controlled trial
claims.quote: Contrary to the Conclusions Stated in the Paper, Only Dry Fat-Free Mass Was Different between Groups upon Reanalysis. Comment on: "Intermittent Energy Restriction Attenuates the Loss of Fat-Free Mass in Resistance Trained Individuals. A Randomized Controlled Trial".
claims.journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology

claims.statement: Across 49 randomised trials of resistance training lasting six weeks or more, adding protein kept improving fat-free mass only up to a total intake of about 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight per day; past that point extra protein added nothing further to fat-free mass.
claims.amount: breakpoint at 1.62 g/kg bodyweight/day; 49 studies, 1863 participants, resistance training >=6 weeks
claims.population: Healthy adults of both sexes, spanning young and older and both trained and untrained, in energy balance, doing prolonged supervised resistance training; the effect was larger in already resistance-trained individuals and smaller with increasing age
claims.quote: Protein supplementation beyond total protein intakes of 1.62 g/kg/day resulted in no further RET-induced gains in FFM.

claims.statement: A meta-analysis of 74 randomised trials found that eating more protein gives only small extra lean-mass gains, and in adults under 65 doing resistance exercise the benefit appeared only at intakes of 1.6 g/kg/day or above.
claims.amount: >=1.6 g/kg/day in adults <65 y; 1.2-1.59 g/kg/day in adults >=65 y; 74 RCTs, 62 of them involving resistance exercise; pooled SMD for lean body mass 0.22
claims.population: Healthy, non-obese adults of both sexes, mostly untrained to recreationally trained, generally in energy balance, most enrolled in resistance exercise training programmes
claims.quote: The effect on LBM was significant in subjects >=65 years old ingesting 1.2-1.59 g of protein/kg/day and for younger subjects (<65 years old) ingesting >=1.6 g of protein/kg/day submitted to RE.
claims.journal: Journal of cachexia, sarcopenia and muscle

claims.statement: Pooling 105 trials, each additional 0.1 g/kg/day of protein was worth about 0.39 kg of lean mass while total intake was below 1.3 g/kg/day, but only about 0.12 kg once above it - returns shrink roughly three-fold past that point.
claims.amount: 0.39 kg vs 0.12 kg lean mass per +0.1 g/kg/day, below vs above 1.3 g/kg/day; doses spanned 0.5 to 3.5 g/kg/d; 105 articles, 5402 participants, interventions of several months
claims.population: Mixed adult populations across 105 RCTs (healthy and clinical, trained and untrained, both sexes, wide age range), predominantly not in a deliberate energy deficit
claims.quote: the mean increase in lean body mass associated with an increase in protein intake of 0.1 g/kg of body weight per day was 0.39 kg (95%CI, 0.36-0.41) and 0.12 kg (95%CI, 0.11-0.14) below and above the total protein intake of 1.3 g/kg/d, respectively.

claims.statement: Isotope-tracer measurement in trained male bodybuilders on a rest day put the average protein requirement at 1.7 g/kg/day with an upper recommended intake of 2.2 g/kg/day - roughly 2.6 times the standard RDA.
claims.amount: Estimated Average Requirement 1.7 g/kg/day; upper 95% CI RDA 2.2 g/kg/day; protein intakes tested from 0.1 to 3.5 g/kg/day; 8 men across 42 experiments
claims.population: Eight healthy young male bodybuilders (mean age 22.5 y, 13% body fat, at least 3 years of training), studied at rest on a non-training day, fed at 1.5x measured resting energy expenditure so not in an energy deficit
claims.quote: The Estimated Average Requirement (EAR) of protein and the upper 95% CI RDA for these young male bodybuilders were 1.7 and 2.2 g . kg. d, respectively.

claims.statement: In resistance-trained men already habitually eating a lot of protein, whole-body protein balance on a training day stopped improving at about 2.0 g/kg/day - higher than tracer-derived estimates in non-exercising men.
claims.amount: breakpoint ~2.00 g/kg/day (95% CI 1.62-2.38 for synthesis; 1.44-2.57 for net balance); intakes tested 0.20-3.00 g/kg/day; n=7
claims.population: Seven resistance-trained men (mean age 24 y, 80 kg, 11% body fat, habitual protein intake 2.3 g/kg/day), measured after a whole-body resistance exercise bout under energy-adequate hourly mixed-meal feeding
claims.quote: A breakpoint protein intake of ~2.0 g.kg-1.d-1, which maximized whole-body anabolism in resistance-trained men after exercise, is greater than previous IAAO-derived estimates for nonexercising men and is at the upper range of current general protein recommendations for athletes.

claims.statement: Young men in a severe 40% calorie deficit who ate 2.4 g/kg/day gained 1.2 kg of lean mass over four weeks while those at 1.2 g/kg/day gained essentially none, and the higher-protein group also lost more fat.
claims.amount: 2.4 vs 1.2 g/kg/day for 4 weeks at ~40% energy deficit (33 kcal/kg lean mass/day); lean body mass +1.2 vs +0.1 kg; fat mass -4.8 vs -3.5 kg; n=20 per group
claims.population: 40 young recreationally active men in a 4-week ~40% energy deficit performing resistance training combined with high-intensity interval training six days per week
claims.quote: As a result of the intervention, LBM increased (P < 0.05) in the PRO group (1.2 +/- 1.0 kg) and to a greater extent (P < 0.05) compared with the CON group (0.1 +/- 1.0 kg). The PRO group had a greater loss of fat mass than did the CON group (PRO: -4.8 +/- 1.6 kg; CON: -3.5 +/- 1.4kg; P < 0.05).
claims.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

claims.statement: Resistance-trained athletes cutting to 60% of their usual calories for two weeks lost 1.6 kg of lean mass on 1.0 g/kg/day but only 0.3 kg on 2.3 g/kg/day, with no difference in fat loss or performance between diets.
claims.amount: ~2.3 g/kg/day (35% of energy) vs ~1.0 g/kg/day (15% of energy); 60% of habitual energy intake for 2 weeks; lean body mass -0.3 vs -1.6 kg; n=10 per group
claims.population: 20 young healthy resistance-trained male athletes continuing their habitual training through a 2-week hypoenergetic diet
claims.quote: Total (-3.0 +/- 0.4 and -1.5 +/- 0.3 kg for the CP and HP, respectively, P = 0.036) and lean body mass loss (-1.6 +/- 0.3 and -0.3 +/- 0.3 kg, P = 0.006) were significantly larger in the CP compared with those in the HP.
claims.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

claims.statement: In a controlled 21-day 40% calorie deficit, both 1.6 and 2.4 g/kg/day protected fat-free mass better than the 0.8 g/kg/day RDA - but 2.4 was no better than 1.6, suggesting the protective effect plateaus near twice the RDA.
claims.amount: 0.8 vs 1.6 vs 2.4 g/kg/day for 31 days (10 days weight maintenance then 21 days at a 40% energy deficit); mean weight loss 3.2 kg; n=39
claims.population: 39 adults, men and women, described only as adults rather than as trained athletes, in a controlled 21-day 40% energy deficit with no prescribed resistance training programme
claims.quote: The proportion of weight loss due to reductions in fat-free mass was lower (P<0.05) and the loss of fat mass was higher (P<0.05) in those receiving 2x-RDA and 3x-RDA compared to RDA.
claims.journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology

claims.statement: A meta-analysis of 22 comparisons found protein above the RDA helps lean mass only when the body is stressed: it preserved 0.36 kg during calorie restriction and added 0.77 kg with resistance training, but did essentially nothing (0.08 kg) in people neither dieting nor lifting.
claims.amount: protein above 0.8 g/kg/day vs at 0.8 g/kg/day; +0.36 kg under energy restriction (14 comparisons), +0.77 kg with resistance training (3 comparisons), +0.08 kg unstressed (7 comparisons); trials >=6 weeks; 18 studies
claims.population: Apparently healthy adults aged 19 and over of both sexes in randomised parallel trials of at least six weeks, subgrouped by whether they were energy restricted, resistance training, both, or neither
claims.quote: protein intakes greater than the RDA attenuated lean mass loss after ER [0.36 (0.06, 0.67) kg, n = 14], increased lean mass after resistance training (RT) [0.77 (0.23, 1.31) kg, n = 3], but did not differentially affect changes in lean mass [0.08 (-0.59, 0.75) kg, n = 7] under nonstressed conditions (no ER + no RT).

claims.statement: A systematic review of six studies in lean, energy-restricted resistance-trained athletes concluded protein needs are likely 2.3-3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass per day, rising with how lean the athlete is and how steep the deficit is.
claims.amount: 2.3-3.1 g/kg fat-free mass/day; 6 studies covering 13 study groups; body fat ceilings of 23% for men and 35% for women; body fat fell 0.5-6.6% and fat-free mass fell 0.3-2.7 kg across groups
claims.population: Adults 18 and over, resistance-trained for more than six months, with low body fat (men <=23%, women <=35%), in energy restriction; this is a systematic review producing a practitioner recommendation, not a head-to-head dose-ranging trial
claims.quote: Protein needs for energy-restricted resistance-trained athletes are likely 2.3-3.1g/kg of FFM scaled upwards with severity of caloric restriction and leanness.
claims.journal: International journal of sport nutrition and exercise metabolism

claims.statement: In roughly 80 kg resistance-trained young men, 20 g of whey after leg exercise raised muscle protein synthesis about as much as 40 g did; the extra 20 g mainly increased amino acid burning and urea production.
claims.amount: 0, 10, 20 or 40 g whey protein isolate immediately after exercise; myofibrillar synthesis rose 49% at 20 g and 56% at 40 g over 4 hours; n=48
claims.population: 48 resistance-trained young men averaging about 80 kg, in energy balance, after a standardised high-protein breakfast and a unilateral leg resistance exercise bout
claims.quote: A 20-g dose of whey protein is sufficient for the maximal stimulation of postabsorptive rates of myofibrillar MPS in rested and exercised muscle of ~80-kg resistance-trained, young men. A dose of whey protein >20 g stimulates amino acid oxidation and ureagenesis.
claims.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

claims.statement: When the training session works the whole body rather than one leg, 40 g of whey stimulated more muscle protein synthesis than 20 g - and how much lean mass a person carried did not change which dose worked better.
claims.amount: 20 g vs 40 g whey after whole-body resistance exercise; muscle protein synthesis 0.059 vs 0.049 %/h (P = 0.005); n=30, split into groups with <=65 kg and >=70 kg lean body mass
claims.population: 30 resistance-trained young men stratified by lean body mass (15 with <=65 kg, 15 with >=70 kg), in energy balance, after a single bout of whole-body resistance exercise
claims.quote: Our data indicate that ingestion of 40 g whey protein following whole-body resistance exercise stimulates a greater MPS response than 20 g in young resistance-trained men. However, with the current doses, the total amount of LBM does not seem to influence the response.

claims.statement: A quadruple-tracer study found no upper limit to the anabolic response to a single meal: 100 g of protein after exercise produced a larger and longer-lasting response (beyond 12 hours) than 25 g, and the surplus was not simply oxidised away.
claims.amount: 100 g vs 25 g protein in a single post-exercise meal; anabolic response tracked for more than 12 hours
claims.population: Humans recovering from a bout of exercise, studied in vivo with a feeding-infusion tracer protocol; the retrieved abstract does not state sex, age, training status or energy state, and this is an acute single-meal study rather than a training trial
claims.quote: Using a comprehensive quadruple isotope tracer feeding-infusion approach, we show that the ingestion of 100 g protein results in a greater and more prolonged (>12 h) anabolic response when compared to the ingestion of 25 g protein.

claims.statement: Splitting 80 g of whey into four 20 g servings every three hours stimulated 31-48% more muscle protein synthesis across 12 hours of post-exercise recovery than either eight 10 g servings or two 40 g servings.
claims.amount: 80 g whey over 12 h delivered as 8 x 10 g every 1.5 h, 4 x 20 g every 3 h, or 2 x 40 g every 6 h; the 4 x 20 g pattern was 31-48% higher; n=24 (8 per group)
claims.population: 24 healthy trained young males in energy balance, across 12 hours of recovery from a single resistance exercise bout
claims.quote: All ingestion protocols increased MPS above rest throughout 1-12 h recovery (88-148%, P < 0.02), but INT elicited greater MPS than PULSE and BOLUS (31-48%, P < 0.02).

claims.statement: Spreading the same daily protein evenly across three meals of about 30 g each produced 25% higher 24-hour muscle protein synthesis than loading most of it into dinner, and the advantage persisted after a week on the diet.
claims.amount: even pattern of ~31.5 / 29.9 / 32.7 g vs skewed ~10.7 / 16.0 / 63.4 g at breakfast, lunch and dinner; 24-h fractional synthesis rate 0.075 vs 0.056 %/h; 7-day crossover with 30-day washout; n=8
claims.population: 8 healthy weight-stable adult men and women, mean age 37, BMI 25.7, with no resistance training programme, in a controlled isoenergetic and isonitrogenous crossover feeding study
claims.quote: The 24-h mixed muscle protein fractional synthesis rate was 25% higher in the EVEN (0.075 +/- 0.006%/h) vs. the SKEW (0.056 +/- 0.006%/h) protein distribution groups (P = 0.003).

claims.statement: Over 16 weeks of dieting plus resistance training, splitting protein evenly across three meals versus skewing it to dinner made no difference to lean mass, fat loss or thigh muscle area.
claims.amount: 90 g protein/day (1.0 g/kg/day) given as even 30/30/30 g or skewed 10/20/60 g; 750 kcal/day deficit; 16 weeks; resistance training 3 days/week; n=41; lean mass fell 1.0 kg and fat mass 6.9 kg in both arms
claims.population: 41 men and women, mean age 35, mean BMI 31.5, i.e. overweight or obese adults new to structured training rather than lean trained athletes, in a 750 kcal/day energy deficit with resistance training three days per week
claims.quote: The effectiveness of dietary energy restriction combined with resistance training to improve body composition is not influenced by the within-day distribution of protein when adequate total protein is consumed.
claims.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

claims.statement: Reviewing both acute and long-term data, two sports-nutrition researchers concluded there is no hard per-meal ceiling and recommended aiming for 0.4 g per kg of bodyweight per meal across at least four meals, rising to about 0.55 g/kg/meal for someone targeting 2.2 g/kg/day.
claims.amount: 0.4 g/kg/meal across a minimum of four meals to reach 1.6 g/kg/day; up to 0.55 g/kg/meal if targeting the upper reported daily intake of 2.2 g/kg/day
claims.population: Adults engaged in regimented resistance training; this is a narrative review that synthesises acute tracer studies and longer training trials into a practical heuristic, not new data
claims.quote: Based on the current evidence, we conclude that to maximize anabolism one should consume protein at a target intake of 0.4 g/kg/meal across a minimum of four meals
claims.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

claims.statement: Trained men and women who pushed protein to 3.4 g/kg/day alongside a periodised heavy lifting programme lost more fat than a 2.3 g/kg/day group despite eating more total calories - but gained exactly the same fat-free mass, 1.5 kg in both groups.
claims.amount: 3.4 vs 2.3 g/kg/day for 8 weeks; fat-free mass +1.5 kg in both groups; fat mass -1.7 kg (high protein) vs -0.3 kg (normal protein); body fat -2.4% vs -0.7%; n=48 (31 high protein, 17 normal protein; 11 women in total)
claims.population: 48 healthy resistance-trained men and women (mean age 23-25, 2-5 years of training) on a split-routine periodised heavy resistance training programme; diets were self-recorded rather than provided, and the high-protein group also consumed significantly more total energy
claims.quote: There was a significant time effect for FFM; however, there was a non-significant time by group effect for FFM (change: +1.5 +/- 1.8 NP, +1.5 +/- 2.2 HP).
claims.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

claims.statement: Pooling 28 trials in 1358 adults without kidney disease, high-protein diets did not worsen the change in kidney filtration rate compared with lower-protein diets, though filtration rate measured at the end of the intervention was trivially higher.
claims.amount: high protein defined as >=1.5 g/kg bodyweight, or >=20% of energy, or >=100 g/day; trials longer than 4 days; 28 studies, 1358 participants
claims.population: Adults without kidney disease across 28 randomised controlled trials, both sexes, mixed training status and mixed energy states; the analysis notes an unclear risk of selection bias in the included trials
claims.quote: Our analysis indicates that HP intakes do not adversely influence kidney function on GFR in healthy adults.

claims.statement: In rats held at a 40% calorie restriction for 16 weeks, muscle protein content fell 38% and anabolic mTORC1 signalling was suppressed regardless of whether the diet supplied 10% or 32% protein - a caution that protein's protective effect in short human diets may not carry over to long, deep deficits.
claims.amount: 40% calorie restriction for 16 weeks; adequate (10%) vs high (32%) protein milk-based diets; muscle protein content 38% lower under restriction
claims.population: Twelve-week-old male Sprague Dawley rats, not humans; ad libitum versus 40% calorie-restricted feeding, adequate versus high protein, 16 weeks, with no exercise intervention
claims.quote: Independent of dietary protein intake, muscle protein content was 38% lower (< 0.05) in CR compared to AL.

claims.statement: Creatine taken alongside resistance training adds roughly 1.4 kg of lean tissue over and above training alone in older adults, with smaller but real gains in chest press and leg press strength.
claims.amount: Creatine vs placebo during resistance training 2-3 days/week for 7-52 weeks; per-study creatine doses not specified in the abstract
claims.population: 721 randomised participants across 22 RCTs, men and women, mean age 57-70 years across studies
claims.quote: Creatine supplementation resulted in greater increases in lean tissue mass (mean difference =1.37 kg [95% CI =0.97-1.76];<0.00001), chest press strength (standardized mean difference [SMD] =0.35 [0.16-0.53];=0.0002), and leg press strength (SMD =0.24 [0.05-0.43];=0.01).
claims.journal: Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine

claims.statement: In adults under 50, creatine added to resistance training increases lean body mass by about 1.1 kg and modestly reduces fat mass compared with the same training without creatine; taking it with carbohydrate adds nothing.
claims.amount: 7 g/day, or 0.3 g/kg body mass per day; 12 RCTs pooled, resistance training programmes of varying length
claims.population: Adults younger than 50 years undertaking resistance training; 12 studies pooled, both trained and untrained subgroups analysed
claims.quote: Compared with resistance training (RT) alone, creatine supplementation increased LBM by 1.14 kg (95% CI 0.69 to 1.59), and reduced body fat percentage by -0.88% (95% CI -1.66 to -0.11) and body fat mass by -0.73 kg (95% CI -1.34 to -0.11). There were no differences between training status or carbohydrate subgroups.
claims.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research

claims.statement: The ISSN position stand concludes creatine is safe long term at doses far above what most people take, and that a low habitual intake may itself be worthwhile across the lifespan.
claims.amount: Up to 30 g/day for up to 5 years studied; habitual low intake ~3 g/day suggested
claims.population: Healthy individuals and patient populations ranging from infants to the elderly, as reviewed by the International Society of Sports Nutrition
claims.quote: These studies show that short and long-term supplementation (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) is safe and well-tolerated in healthy individuals and in a number of patient populations ranging from infants to the elderly. Moreover, significant health benefits may be provided by ensuring habitual low dietary creatine ingestion (e.g., 3 g/day) throughout the lifespan.
claims.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

claims.statement: DOES NOT WORK: creatyl-L-leucine, a marketed 'advanced' creatine derivative, failed to raise muscle creatine content at all, while plain creatine monohydrate at the same dose did. The novel form performed identically to placebo.
claims.amount: 5 g/day for 14 days, with three supervised resistance exercise sessions per week; muscle biopsies before and after
claims.population: 29 healthy adults (17 men, 12 women, mean age ~28-30 years) in a randomised double-blind trial
claims.quote: Cr monohydrate supplementation which significantly increased muscle Cr content with 14 days of supplementation. No changes in muscle Cr were observed for the placebo or CLL groups. Cr monohydrate supplementation is an effective strategy to augment muscle Cr content while CLL is not.
claims.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism

claims.statement: Across 21 published meta-analyses, caffeine improved strength, muscle endurance, power and aerobic endurance, but the evidence was graded only moderate quality and some analyses could not confirm the direction of effect once prediction intervals were considered.
claims.amount: Doses varied across the 21 pooled meta-analyses; not standardised in this umbrella review
claims.population: 11 systematic reviews containing 21 meta-analyses; most primary studies were conducted among young men
claims.quote: In the meta-analyses, caffeine was ergogenic for aerobic endurance, muscle strength, muscle endurance, power, jumping performance and exercise speed. However, not all analyses provided a definite direction for the effect of caffeine when considering the 95% prediction interval.

claims.statement: The effective caffeine dose is 3-6 mg per kg bodyweight taken about an hour before training; going up to 9 mg/kg adds side effects without adding performance.
claims.amount: 3-6 mg/kg body mass, most commonly 60 minutes pre-exercise; minimum effective dose possibly as low as 2 mg/kg
claims.population: Trained and untrained individuals, as reviewed in the ISSN position stand on caffeine and exercise performance
claims.quote: Caffeine has consistently been shown to improve exercise performance when consumed in doses of 3-6 mg/kg body mass. Minimal effective doses of caffeine currently remain unclear but they may be as low as 2 mg/kg body mass. Very high doses of caffeine (e.g. 9 mg/kg) are associated with a high incidence of side-effects and do not seem to be required to elicit an ergogenic effect.
claims.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

claims.statement: Beta-alanine works for efforts lasting roughly one to four minutes by buffering muscle acidity, and needs several weeks of daily loading to work at all. The ISSN itself states the strength evidence is not there yet.
claims.amount: 4-6 g daily for at least 2-4 weeks; divided lower doses of 1.6 g reduce the tingling side effect
claims.population: Healthy populations reviewed by the International Society of Sports Nutrition
claims.quote: Daily supplementation with 4 to 6 g of beta-alanine for at least 2 to 4 weeks has been shown to improve exercise performance, with more pronounced effects in open end-point tasks/time trials lasting 1 to 4 min in duration; ... 7) More research is needed to determine the effects of beta-alanine on strength, endurance performance beyond 25 min in duration, and other health-related benefits associated with carnosine.
claims.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

claims.statement: Pooled across 40 trials the overall beta-alanine effect is small (effect size 0.18) and depends heavily on exercise duration; total amount of beta-alanine ingested did not moderate the effect.
claims.amount: Chronic ingestion protocols only; total amount ingested was not a significant moderator (p=0.438)
claims.population: 1461 participants across 40 double-blind placebo-controlled studies, 65 exercise protocols, all healthy populations, trained and untrained

claims.statement: DOES NOT WORK FOR HYPERTROPHY: in resistance-trained men, eight weeks of full-dose beta-alanine added nothing to strength or muscle thickness gains. The training worked; the supplement contributed nothing measurable.
