gaps.gap: No trial in this evidence base tested whether any dietary change - sodium restriction, DASH, fibre, or a saturated-to-unsaturated fat swap - can offset lipid or blood-pressure changes caused by exogenous androgens, anabolic steroids, or any other performance or physique compound. Every effect size above comes from people whose lipids and blood pressure are diet- and disease-driven, not compound-driven.

The androgen literature (PMID 34481638) reports that testosterone therapy raises blood pressure and lowers HDL, but no study measured whether a diet intervention layered on top of that changes the trajectory; the two literatures have never been combined.

Oral 17-alpha-alkylated androgens are the class most associated with HDL suppression and hepatic enzyme elevation, yet no controlled feeding trial found here recruited users of them, so no effect size exists for diet in that group.

Nothing establishes whether a compound-driven HDL drop responds to diet at all. Because the mechanism (hepatic lipase upregulation) differs from diet-driven dyslipidaemia, the LDL and HDL effect sizes reported here cannot be assumed to transfer.

Liver-marker evidence is almost entirely about hepatic fat and ALT/AST/GGT in metabolic fatty liver disease. No study here separates a diet-driven transaminase rise from a compound-driven or exercise-driven one, and none addresses whether creatine kinase-confounded ALT in heavy lifters behaves the same way.

Sodium's effect on blood pressure is well quantified for treated hypertension and for untreated adults, but not for young, lean, heavily training people with normal-to-high-normal blood pressure - the demographic most likely to be using this kind of app.

The DASH pattern's blood-pressure effect was only reliably demonstrated when food was supplied (PMID 38804177); the effect size for self-directed DASH adherence, which is what an app can actually support, is essentially unestablished.

Ultra-processed food evidence for lipids and blood pressure specifically is either a single 20-person 2-week inpatient trial (PMID 31105044, which measured energy intake and weight, not a lipid panel or blood pressure as primary outcomes) or observational cohorts. No medium-term randomised trial reports what removing ultra-processed food does to LDL, blood pressure or ALT.

The alcohol-blood-pressure threshold (no benefit below two drinks/day) comes from a population that was 86% male but is not stratified by body size, training status or concurrent hormone use; whether the same threshold applies at different lean masses is unknown.

Fibre-to-blood-pressure evidence rests on six small human trials (PMID 40806090) and loses significance in mixed populations; the fibre dose in grams per day needed for a given mmHg change is not established.
No study identified reports how long a favourable lipid or liver-marker change persists after a dietary change stops, or how it interacts with a compound cycle's on/off phases.

Sex- and hormone-status-stratified effect sizes are largely missing: most feeding trials report pooled results, and none stratify by circulating androgen or oestrogen level, so the app cannot personalise expected effect sizes by hormonal context.

No adequately powered trial has compared a range of surplus sizes (e.g. 5% vs 10% vs 20%) head-to-head in trained lifters with gold-standard body composition measurement. The one direct attempt (PMID 37914977) was cut to 17 completers by COVID-19 and used skinfolds and ultrasound rather than DXA or a 4-component model, so the 'optimal surplus' remains an inference, not a measured result.

No study establishes an optimal RATE of weight gain. The often-quoted ~0.5%/week figure traces to a single-arm regression in 21 overfed men over 6 weeks (PMID 33919267) whose authors state that changes in outcome variables 'could generally not be predicted with precision' (Bayes R-squared 0.18-0.40). The 0.25-0.5%/week and 0.45 kg/week numbers in circulation are expert opinion (PMIDs 31247944, 35233712), not trial endpoints.

Nothing longer than about 12 weeks exists. Every surplus/bulking trial retrieved ran 4-12 weeks, so the literature says nothing about the 6-12 month timescale on which people actually run a gaining phase, whether early lean gains persist, or whether the muscle-to-fat ratio degrades as the phase continues.

POPULATION MISMATCH: none of the energy-surplus or rate-of-gain trials studied people using anabolic-androgenic steroids, SARMs, growth hormone or other anabolic compounds. Participants were described as drug-free or their status was simply not reported. The only supraphysiologic-androgen trial retrieved (PMID 8637535) did not manipulate energy intake at all, so the interaction between surplus size and anabolic drug use is completely unstudied.

POPULATION MISMATCH: no retrieved study examined bulking, surplus size or rate of gain in people on gender-affirming hormone therapy, testosterone replacement therapy, or any exogenous hormone regimen. Whether these surplus and rate targets transfer to someone whose androgen or oestrogen status is being actively changed is unknown, and the direction of any error is not predictable from the existing data.

Women are badly under-represented. The largest hypertrophy meta-analysis retrieved (PMID 32079265) is males only; several core trials are male-only (PMIDs 26957922, 31915482, 33919267); and no retrieved trial reports the effect of surplus size or rate of gain separately by sex, so sex-specific targets are unsupported.

No trial has tested whether starting body-fat percentage should change the surplus prescription in resistance trainees. The 60-70%-vs-30-40% lean partitioning data (PMID 10865771) come from general overfeeding experiments without a training stimulus, so applying them to lifters is an extrapolation.

Measurement quality undermines several of the key numbers: bioelectrical impedance (PMID 42442697), skinfolds (PMID 37914977) and air displacement plethysmography (PMID 24834017) are poorly suited to resolving ~1 kg fat-free mass changes over 8-12 weeks. 'Fat-free mass' also includes water and glycogen, which rise with carbohydrate and calorie intake independently of contractile tissue.

The composition of the surplus is unresolved. Surplus calories from protein alone appeared inert for both muscle and fat (PMID 24834017), while extra carbohydrate matched protein+carbohydrate (PMID 12094125), and one large-surplus trial found fat gain without significant lean gain (PMID 26957922). No trial has held surplus size constant while varying macronutrient source with a direct hypertrophy outcome in trained lifters.

No study establishes a physiological ceiling on how fast lean mass CAN be gained. Every rate figure available is a group mean from a fixed-duration training study, not a measurement of a maximum, and the 10-fold and 3-fold individual variability documented under controlled overfeeding (PMIDs 9880251, 2336074) means group means can badly misrepresent any individual.

There is no evidence on periodised gaining: whether alternating surplus and maintenance blocks, or interrupting a bulk with a short deficit, improves the muscle-to-fat ratio compared with a continuous surplus has not been tested in any retrieved trial.

There is no validated way to individualise a surplus prospectively. The one study that explicitly tried to predict who gains lean versus fat from baseline characteristics, physical activity and dietary intake failed to do so (PMID 33919267), which means the only defensible method is adjusting the surplus against a measured rate of gain, and even the target rate is not evidence-based.

No randomised trial has compared weekly rates of loss (e.g. 0.5% vs 1.0% vs 1.5% of bodyweight) in already-lean resistance-trained lifters. The single controlled rate trial (Garthe, PMID 21558571) used mixed-sport elite athletes at a normal body-fat level, so the 0.7%/week figure is an extrapolation when applied to contest-lean physique athletes.

Nothing in this literature was studied in people using anabolic-androgenic steroids or other anabolic compounds. Every rate, deficit and protein trial retrieved either specified drug-free participants (natural bodybuilding and physique cohorts) or did not screen for enhancement, so the deficit size and rate of loss at which enhanced lifters start losing lean mass is entirely unestablished.

Whether men on TRT are protected from cutting-induced lean-mass loss has not been tested in lean, trained men. The only testosterone-plus-diet RCT retrieved (PMID 27716209) enrolled middle-aged obese men with low testosterone on a very-low-energy diet with no structured resistance training - and even there testosterone did not prevent lean-mass loss during the diet phase itself.

No trial has tested weight-loss rate, deficit size, protein intake or resistance training as manipulated variables in people losing weight on GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists. The body-composition evidence there is drug-versus-comparator meta-analysis, so it cannot say whether a slower titration or higher protein changes the ~25% lean-mass fraction.

The 30 kcal per kg fat-free mass per day energy-availability threshold rests on 5-day laboratory studies in young, sedentary, regularly menstruating women. No equivalent validated threshold exists for men, for trained athletes, or for exposures lasting weeks to months rather than days.

There is no established energy-availability or deficit threshold for lean-mass and strength loss specifically. The threshold work targets reproductive and bone endpoints; the muscle-relevant number (~500 kcal/day, PMID 34623696) comes from meta-regression across heterogeneous trials, not from a dose-ranging experiment.

No dose-response data link a specific weekly rate of loss to a specific probability of menstrual disturbance, testosterone suppression, T3 fall or bone-marker change. Practitioners cannot currently say what percentage per week keeps a given individual above threshold.

Almost nothing has been studied in adolescents, masters/older lifters, post-menopausal women, or transgender people on gender-affirming hormone therapy while in a deficit - all populations where hormonal endpoints of a cut would be expected to differ.

Controlled diets in this literature run about 2-25 weeks. There is no evidence on safe cumulative dieting duration, how many cuts per year are tolerable, or how long hormonal and bone recovery takes beyond roughly 12 months of follow-up.

Whether diet breaks and refeeds actually preserve lean mass in trained lifters is unresolved: the ICECAP RCT (PMID 33587549) found no fat-free-mass advantage over continuous restriction, and the diet-break meta-analysis (PMID 38193357) found the resting-metabolic-rate benefit was smaller in resistance-trained people than in people with overweight/obesity.

Most physique-specific evidence is uncontrolled case studies or small non-randomised cohorts, and body-composition estimates rely on DXA, BIA or skinfolds, whose error at very low body fat and under glycogen and hydration shifts is large relative to the lean-mass differences being claimed.

No study has validated a monitoring protocol - resting heart rate, RMR ratio, T3, leptin, menstrual status - as a way for an individual to titrate their deficit in real time and avoid crossing into REDs; the IOC tool stratifies risk after the fact rather than guiding day-to-day deficit adjustment.

No completed randomized trial has tested whether a specific protein intake preserves lean mass during GLP-1 therapy. The trial designed to answer it (LEAN-PREP, NCT06885736, PMID 42020128, 1.6 g/kg/day) has published only a protocol; every protein number in circulation is extrapolated from general weight-loss and sarcopenia literature, not measured on these drugs.

Nobody has studied resistance-trained people or physique athletes on GLP-1 receptor agonists. PubMed searches pairing GLP-1 agonists with resistance-trained, athlete, bodybuilder or physique populations returned zero results; every body-composition trial recruited unselected or sedentary adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes at high starting BMI. The single mention of a trained population is a secondary reference in a review (PMID 41577337) to tirzepatide plus resistance and aerobic training in young men, with no primary report retrievable.

GLP-1 receptor agonists used concurrently with testosterone or other anabolic-androgenic steroids are entirely unstudied. A PubMed search for semaglutide with testosterone and anabolic-androgenic steroids returned zero results, so the effect of that combination on lean-mass retention, protein requirements, or GI tolerance is unknown and cannot be inferred from any published trial.

The optimal protein target has never been compared head-to-head under pharmacological appetite suppression. Whether 1.2, 1.6 or 2.0 g/kg/day differ in outcome on a GLP-1 drug, and whether per-meal doses of 0.3-0.4 g/kg are even physically achievable when satiety is drug-driven, has not been tested.

Objective physical function was not reported in any of the 35 randomized trials in the Annals systematic review (PMID 41996180), so whether the measured lean-mass loss translates into any loss of performance, strength or capacity is unestablished.

Body-composition measurement is not comparable across the literature. BIA, DXA, CT and MRI give materially different lean-mass estimates, and heterogeneity was severe enough that the Annals review could not perform a meta-analysis at all - so any single headline percentage is method-dependent.

No randomized trial has tested a dietary strategy against GI side effects. Smaller frequent meals, hydration, avoiding high-fat and high-sugar foods, and fiber are all expert opinion; the systematic review of 16 RCTs (PMID 42037117) found GI symptoms occurred despite background dietary counselling, and no trial has isolated a diet as the intervention.
Dietary fiber supplementation combined with a GLP-1 receptor agonist has never been trialled, including for constipation relief, despite the mechanistic rationale set out in PMID 42106160.
Bone health was not assessed in any of the 16 RCTs in the dietary-strategies systematic review (PMID 42037117), so the skeletal consequences of the diets used alongside these drugs are unquantified.

Whether lean mass lost on a GLP-1 drug returns as lean mass after discontinuation, or is replaced preferentially by fat, has not been measured directly in a randomized trial; preferential fat regain is hypothesised rather than demonstrated.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide showed materially different lean-mass proportions in meta-analysis (35.2% vs 25.4%, PMID 41877354), but whether protein or training requirements should therefore differ by compound has never been studied.

There is no lean-mass or nutrition data in lean or near-lean individuals using these compounds for body-composition or aesthetic purposes. All body-composition evidence comes from populations with obesity (mean BMI 27.9-41.6) or type 2 diabetes, so extrapolation to a low-body-fat user is unsupported.

Almost none of the dietary-adherence and self-monitoring literature is in trained or physique-focused populations. The foundational reviews sample adults with overweight or obesity in clinical weight-management programmes - historically predominantly white women - and report nothing about lifters, competitors, or people managing body composition while already lean.

No trial has tested meal prepping itself - batch-cooking and pre-portioning several days of food in advance - as an intervention. The supporting evidence for meal planning and home cooking is cross-sectional and confounded by income, time, food skills and health motivation, so the causal direction is unknown.

The per-meal protein and leucine 'thresholds' come from acute muscle-protein-synthesis measurements over a few hours, not from trials showing that hitting them repeatedly changes muscle mass or strength over months. The one long trial that matched total daily protein found source made no difference to outcomes.

Leucine dose-response data come from isolated protein powders and beverages. No equivalent threshold has been established for whole mixed meals as actually eaten, where fat, fibre and slower gastric emptying change amino-acid appearance in the blood.

Whether the smaller acute anabolic response to plant proteins matters in practice, once total daily protein is adequate, is unresolved: the only medium-term comparison was small, in previously untrained young men, and allocated groups by habitual diet rather than randomising them.

There is no established fibre target for satiety. The doses shown to cut acute energy intake are isolated supplemental fibres (guar gum, alginate, polydextrose, beta-glucan), not whole-food fibre, and no trial has tested a grams-per-day whole-food fibre target against hunger or adherence during an energy deficit.

Optimal diet-break and refeed parameters - duration, frequency, and how far calories should rise - are not established. The two best trials used incompatible structures (2-week blocks at 67% of maintenance versus 1-week breaks after 3-week blocks) and disagree on whether the structure improves body composition at all.

Diet-break and refeed evidence in trained people rests on a handful of small trials, at least one of which has a published independent reanalysis disputing its conclusions. No trial has run diet breaks through to a competition-level body-fat endpoint, where the metabolic and psychological pressures are greatest.

Energy-density research is almost entirely short laboratory meals and 6-to-12-month behavioural trials in adults with overweight or obesity. Nothing tests whether lowering energy density preserves training performance, lean mass or recovery in people who train hard.

Self-reported intake under-reports true intake by an amount that varies between individuals with body size, dietary restraint and socioeconomic status. No study establishes how accurate any given person's own logging is, so calorie targets built on self-reported intake are systematically optimistic and cannot be individually calibrated from the log alone.

Essentially no adherence, satiety or meal-structure evidence exists in people on exogenous hormone therapy. How oestrogen, testosterone, or incretin-based agents alter hunger, satiety, protein needs and the ability to stick to a prepared plan has not been studied in these designs.

Sex-disaggregated adherence data are sparse and confounded. Several of the strongest energy-density and portion-control trials enrolled women only, the largest intermittent-restriction trial enrolled men only, and the trained-population trials mixed sexes without powering for sex differences - so sex effects on the mechanics of sticking to a plan cannot be separated from differences between trials.

No randomised trial has tested any protein intake against another in people using exogenous testosterone, anabolic-androgenic steroids, SARMs or other anabolic compounds. Every dose-response study above either excluded such users or did not report their use, so the ~1.6 g/kg ceiling and the 2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM deficit range are entirely untested in that population, and it is unknown whether an anabolic compound raises the useful ceiling, lowers it, or leaves it unchanged.

No trial has tested whether higher protein intake preserves lean mass in people losing weight on GLP-1 receptor agonists or GLP-1/GIP dual agonists. Body-composition meta-analyses in that population document substantial lean-mass loss but did not manipulate protein intake, and GLP-1-induced appetite suppression makes hitting 1.6-2.4 g/kg/day a practical problem that no study has addressed.

Nothing establishes a protein target for people on gender-affirming hormone therapy of any kind. Protein requirement studies stratify by birth sex with untreated endogenous hormone status only; no requirement estimate exists for people on testosterone or on oestradiol plus an anti-androgen.

The tracer studies producing the highest requirement estimates (1.7-2.2 g/kg/day in bodybuilders, ~2.0 g/kg/day post-exercise) rest on 8 and 7 participants respectively, all young men. Neither has been replicated in women, in older lifters, or during an energy deficit.

There is almost no sex-stratified dose-response data in resistance-trained women. The large meta-analyses pool both sexes without reporting a separate threshold for women, and the energy-deficit trials that anchor the 2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM recommendation were run predominantly or entirely in men.

Whether the acute superiority of 100 g over 25 g in a single meal translates into more muscle over weeks of training has never been tested. No training trial has compared a few very large protein meals against many moderate ones with hypertrophy as the outcome, so the acute tracer finding and the practical per-meal heuristics remain unreconciled.

The per-meal distribution trials disagree and none was run in the population that cares most. The null result came from overweight adults eating only 1.0 g/kg/day, while the positive results were short-term synthesis measurements rather than muscle-mass outcomes; no distribution trial exists in lean, resistance-trained people in an energy deficit at 2+ g/kg/day.

No trial has tested whether the ~1.6 g/kg breakpoint moves upward for people who are already very lean, very muscular, or many years into training. The meta-regression found that training experience increases the benefit of supplementation but did not identify a separate threshold for advanced lifters.

There is no randomised head-to-head trial comparing intakes above ~2.4 g/kg/day against 1.6-2.0 g/kg/day for lean-mass retention in an energy deficit. The widely quoted 2.3-3.1 g/kg FFM figure is extrapolated from a systematic review of six heterogeneous studies, not derived from a dose-ranging experiment.

Long-term safety at very high intakes rests on thin data: the longest controlled observation above 3 g/kg/day is a one-year crossover in 14 men, and no trial has tracked kidney, bone or cardiovascular endpoints at these intakes over multiple years, in women, or in people with reduced kidney reserve.

The reported fat-loss advantage of very high protein (3.4 g/kg/day) has not been mechanistically explained or replicated under controlled feeding. The trial reporting it relied on self-recorded diet logs rather than provided food, and the high-protein group differed in total energy intake as well as protein.

Effects on strength and function are weaker and less certain than effects on mass. Meta-analyses grade the strength evidence as low quality and find unclear effects on handgrip and only marginal effects on physical-function tests, so a protein target chosen to maximise lean mass may not translate into performance gains.

Nothing here was studied alongside anabolic compounds. PubMed searches combining creatine supplementation with testosterone therapy or anabolic-androgenic steroids in randomised trials returned zero results. Whether creatine, caffeine, beta-alanine, citrulline, HMB or protein add to, blunt, or interact with exogenous testosterone or other hormone therapy is entirely unstudied - any claim of synergy with a hormone protocol is unsupported by randomised human evidence.

No randomised trial establishes how any of these supplements behave in people on gender-affirming hormone therapy. The ISSN female-athlete position stand (PMID 37221858) states outright that evidence for sex-specific supplementation is lacking due to the paucity of female-specific research, and the caffeine umbrella review (PMID 30926628) notes most primary studies were conducted among young men.

Published contamination rates cannot be applied to a specific product a user buys. The 38% figure (PMID 34211326) comes from deliberately selected high-risk products in one national market; it is not an estimate of risk for a randomly chosen mainstream creatine monohydrate or whey tub, and no study has randomised or controlled-tested whether third-party certification programmes actually reduce contamination risk.

The HMB evidence is split along authorship lines and this is unresolved: two independent meta-analyses (PMIDs 29249685, 32456217) found no effect in trained athletes or young adults, while the 2024 ISSN position stand recommending 38 mg/kg/day (PMID 39699070) was co-authored by employees of an HMB manufacturer. There is no independent replication of the large HMB effects reported in industry-linked trials.

Beta-alanine's effect on maximal strength and hypertrophy specifically is not established. An 8-week RCT in trained men found no benefit (PMID 36636181) while a 5-week RCT reported power gains (PMID 29713250, retrieved but not claimed here); the ISSN stand itself calls for more research on strength (PMID 26175657).

Dose-response and optimal timing for citrulline malate are not established. The only pooled strength analysis contained just four trials (PMID 34176406) and the repetition analysis eight (PMID 34010809); no trial has established a threshold dose or tested chronic rather than acute administration for hypertrophy.

No head-to-head randomised trial establishes whether BCAAs or EAAs add anything over an equivalent dose of complete protein at matched leucine content. Wolfe (PMID 28852372) found no human study quantifying muscle protein synthesis after oral BCAAs alone, so even the mechanistic baseline is missing.

Long-term randomised data are absent for every supplement here. Creatine trials in the pooled analyses ran 4-52 weeks; the whey protein meta-analysis in trained individuals (PMID 26403469) noted no studies with an intervention longer than 12 weeks. Whether gains persist, plateau, or reverse over years is unknown.

Whether creatine's measured lean-mass gain is contractile tissue or intracellular water is not resolved by these trials, which used DXA and similar whole-body methods rather than muscle biopsy; the creatine derivative trial (PMID 36007881) that did biopsy measured creatine content, not fibre size.

Interactions between these supplements and prescription medication were not tested in any trial reviewed. Caffeine metabolism is known to vary by CYP1A2 genotype (PMID 33388079) but no trial has stratified dosing by genotype prospectively.

Effects in middle-aged and older women, and in anyone outside the healthy young-male majority of the primary literature, are under-characterised across all seven supplements; the caffeine umbrella review explicitly calls for more primary studies in women, middle-aged and older adults.

Whether multi-ingredient pre-workout blends outperform their individual proven components is not established: a meta-analysis of 35 trials found multi-ingredient protein supplements were not superior when directly compared with protein alone (PMID 30824459), and the tested benefits of blends cannot be attributed to any specific ingredient.

No trial has tested meal timing, meal frequency or eating-window effects in people taking exogenous testosterone, estradiol, or other hormone therapy; every timing study cited here was run in hormonally untreated adults, so effects on body composition under exogenous hormones are unknown.

Whether the significant drops in testosterone and IGF-1 seen with 8-hour eating windows in resistance-trained men (at 8 weeks and again at 12 months) translate into worse long-term muscle, strength or libido outcomes has never been tested as a primary endpoint.

The acute 24-hour muscle-protein-synthesis advantage of evenly distributed protein has never been shown to produce measurably more lean mass in a chronic randomised trial where total daily protein was matched between arms; the distribution literature stops at surrogate biochemical endpoints.

The finding that a 100 g protein bolus has no anabolic ceiling comes from a single acute study in young, recreationally active men; no chronic trial has compared one or two very large protein feedings against the same protein spread across the day for muscle-size outcomes.

Carbohydrate timing around resistance training has not been tested against a hypertrophy or body-composition endpoint in any calorie- and protein-matched trial; the existing carbohydrate-timing evidence is acute performance and glycogen only.

The post-exercise carbohydrate 'window' has not been isolated in athletes who train once a day with 24 hours between sessions - rapid-refeed recommendations derive from studies with under 4 hours between bouts and may not generalise.

Sex-specific timing data are thin: the anabolic-window, protein-distribution and pre-sleep-protein trials enrolled almost exclusively young men, and where women were studied (time-restricted eating in trained females) the fat-mass differences were significant only in per-protocol, not intention-to-treat, analysis.
Whether pre-sleep protein adds anything once total daily protein is equalised remains unresolved, because the trials reporting chronic benefit did not match total protein between groups.

Optimal per-meal protein dose in a large energy deficit, in older adults, and in people with obesity is not established; the 20-40 g per feeding figure comes from young, weight-stable, energy-balanced participants.

Almost every time-restricted-eating trial in trained populations runs 4-12 weeks with DXA as the only body-composition measure; there is one 12-month trial with 20 participants and no data on muscle fibre-level or intramuscular outcomes.

Long-term adherence, dropout and disordered-eating risk of compressed eating windows in physique-focused populations have not been quantified, even though adherence is the most plausible mechanism by which timing rules affect real-world results.
No trial has tested whether meal timing interacts with training time of day - whether an early eating window is better or worse for someone who trains at 8 pm is entirely unstudied.
